title: Targeting Runx1 Slows Cyst Growth in Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease.
abstract: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), the most prevalent hereditary kidney disorder, is characterized by the progressive formation and expansion of kidney cysts that ultimately destroy normal renal parenchyma. Runt-related transcription factor 1 (Runx1), a highly conserved regulator of gene expression, orchestrates diverse cellular signaling pathways. Here, we identify Runx1 as a critical driver of cyst growth in ADPKD. Runx1 expression is markedly upregulated in Pkd1 mutant renal epithelial cells and kidney tissues through a cAMP-dependent mechanism. Pharmacological inhibition of Runx1 with its selective inhibitor, Ro5-3335, significantly attenuates cyst progression in both rapidly and slowly progressive Pkd1 mouse models. Mechanistically, Runx1 enhances proliferation of cyst-lining epithelial cells by activating the AKT-mTOR, MAPK, and STAT3 signaling cascades, while suppressing p53-mediated apoptosis. Moreover, Runx1 promotes macrophage infiltration and inflammatory responses via NF-κB activation and aggravates interstitial fibrosis through the TGF-β/Smad2 pathway. Collectively, these findings uncover Runx1 as a pivotal regulator of cystic disease progression and highlight it as a promising therapeutic target for ADPKD.© 2026 Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology.

llm_summary: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, or ADPKD, is the most common inherited kidney disorder and causes cysts to form and grow in the kidneys until they destroy normal kidney tissue. Researchers discovered that a protein called Runx1, which controls how genes are turned on and off, is abnormally high in kidney cells from people with ADPKD and plays a major role in making cysts grow larger. When scientists used a drug called Ro5-3335 to block Runx1 in mice with ADPKD, the cyst growth slowed down significantly in both fast-progressing and slow-progressing versions of the disease. The team found that Runx1 works by activating multiple growth pathways in the cells that line the cysts, while also turning off natural cell death signals and triggering inflammation and scarring in the kidney tissue. These findings suggest that blocking Runx1 could be a new treatment strategy for ADPKD patients, though more research is needed to test this approach in humans.

llm_summary: Background:  Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, which means the heart's main pumping chamber still works well but the patient still experiences heart failure symptoms, is a growing health problem that affects millions of people worldwide. Recent research suggests that problems in the left atrium, which is the upper chamber of the heart that receives blood from the lungs, may be caused by excess fat tissue in the body rather than by damage to the heart's main pumping function itself.

title: Time-dependent prognostic value of coronary plaque burden and hyperemic myocardial blood flow.
abstract: The time-dependent contributions of coronary atherosclerotic plaque burden and myocardial ischemia to clinical outcomes in suspected coronary artery disease (CAD) remain uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the temporal associations of quantitatively assessed plaque burden and ischemia with cardiovascular events.We studied 1,385 patients with suspected CAD who underwent coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) and [15O]H₂O positron emission tomography (PET) perfusion imaging. Plaque burden was measured as percent atheroma volume (PAV) using AI-based CCTA analysis. Myocardial perfusion was evaluated by regional hyperemic myocardial blood flow (hMBF) using PET. Adjusted Cox regression models, including both PAV and hMBF, were used to assess associations with a composite outcome (death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, unstable angina) at 3, 6, and 9 years.The median follow-up time was 7.1 years, during which 185 patients (13.4%) experienced the outcome. Higher per-patient PAV (per 1%) was consistently and independently associated with increased event rate across all three timepoints (aHR 1.035-1.047, all p < 0.001). Lower regional hMBF (per 0.1 mL/min/g) was independently associated with events at 3 years (aHR 1.050, p = 0.004) and 6 years (aHR 1.028, p = 0.024), but not at 9 years (aHR 1.020, p = 0.063). After excluding early revascularization patients, regional hMBF remained associated with outcomes at all timepoints.Plaque burden and regional hMBF are independent markers of cardiovascular risk. Plaque burden remained consistently associated with adverse clinical outcomes throughout follow-up, whereas regional hMBF was primarily related to short- and intermediate-term events, likely influenced by the effects of myocardial revascularization.© 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether two different measures of heart disease—the amount of plaque buildup in arteries and how well blood flows through heart muscle during stress—could predict which patients would have heart attacks or other serious heart problems. The study followed 1,385 patients with suspected coronary artery disease for about seven years, using special imaging scans to measure plaque buildup and blood flow, then tracked how many patients experienced heart attacks, deaths, or other cardiac events. They found that patients with more plaque buildup in their arteries had a consistently higher risk of heart problems throughout the entire follow-up period, while reduced blood flow was mainly linked to problems in the first few years after testing. The results suggest that plaque buildup is a stable long-term predictor of heart disease risk, whereas blood flow problems may improve after patients receive treatments like stents or bypass surgery. These findings could help doctors better understand which measurements are most important for predicting future heart problems and deciding which patients need more aggressive treatment.

title: Effect of Vutrisiran According to Baseline Tafamidis Use in Transthyretin Amyloidosis With Cardiomyopathy: Insights From HELIOS-B.
abstract: Vutrisiran, an RNA interference therapeutic that suppresses hepatic transthyretin production, improved survival and cardiovascular outcomes in transthyretin amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) in HELIOS-B (A Study to Evaluate Vutrisiran in Patients With Transthyretin Amyloidosis With Cardiomyopathy). Tafamidis, a transthyretin stabilizer, also improves clinical outcomes. Although combining these therapies is mechanistically appealing, clinical evidence supporting this approach is limited.We sought to evaluate whether the treatment effects of vutrisiran differed according to baseline tafamidis use in HELIOS-B.In HELIOS-B, patients with ATTR-CM were randomized to vutrisiran 25 mg or placebo every 3 months for up to 36 months, with tafamidis use permitted and stratified. We assessed treatment effects according to baseline tafamidis use for the primary outcome of all-cause mortality and recurrent cardiovascular events and secondary endpoints, including individual components of the primary outcome, composite of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular events and outpatient worsening heart failure events, functional capacity (6-minute walk distance), and health status (Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire-overall summary score [KCCQ-OSS]).Among 654 participants, 259 (40%) were receiving tafamidis at baseline. Patients on tafamidis were slightly younger and had higher baseline 6-minute walk distance and higher KCCQ-OSS, while baseline characteristics were generally balanced between randomized groups. The treatment effect estimates of vutrisiran compared with placebo for the primary outcome were directionally consistent across baseline tafamidis strata (rate ratio: 0.79 [95% CI: 0.51-1.21] with tafamidis vs 0.67 [95% CI: 0.49-0.93] without), with no statistically significant interaction (Pinteraction = 0.55). Similar patterns were observed for all-cause mortality, cardiovascular events, and outpatient worsening heart failure (all Pinteraction > 0.20), although the magnitudes of the estimated effects were numerically smaller among patients receiving tafamidis at baseline. Vutrisiran preserved 6-minute walk distance in both baseline tafamidis strata (Pinteraction = 0.24), whereas improvement in KCCQ-OSS appeared attenuated among patients receiving tafamidis at baseline.Treatment effect estimates for vutrisiran on clinical outcomes were consistent across baseline tafamidis strata, with no statistically significant interaction according to baseline tafamidis use, with reduced effect size noted in those receiving baseline stabilizers in comparison to monotherapy. These data underscore the need for future prospective studies examining combination therapy in this population. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether combining two different heart medications would work better together for patients with a rare heart disease caused by abnormal protein buildup called transthyretin amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy. The study tested a newer medication called vutrisiran, which works by reducing the production of the harmful protein in the liver, comparing it to a placebo (fake treatment) in 654 patients, some of whom were already taking an older medication called tafamidis that stabilizes the protein. The results showed that vutrisiran improved survival and heart-related outcomes in both groups of patients, whether or not they were already taking tafamidis, though the benefits appeared somewhat smaller in patients who were already on the older medication. The findings suggest that vutrisiran works consistently well as a treatment regardless of whether patients are also using tafamidis, though combining the two medications did not produce dramatically better results than using vutrisiran alone. Researchers concluded that more studies are needed to determine whether combining these two medications is truly the best approach for treating this serious heart condition.

title: Gene Silencer Therapy in Transthyretin Amyloid Cardiomyopathy: A Meta-Analysis of Outcomes Trials.
abstract: Gene-silencing therapies reduce hepatic transthyretin (TTR) production and have been evaluated in phase 3 trials in TTR amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM). However, differences in trial design and background therapies have limited assessment of the overall treatment effect and its consistency according to baseline TTR stabilizer use.To assess the effect of TTR gene-silencing therapies in patients with ATTR-CM.PubMed was searched through June 15, 2026, for randomized, placebo-controlled, phase 3 outcome trials of gene-silencing therapies in ATTR-CM.Two reviewers independently extracted data, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guideline. Fixed-effects meta-analysis estimated rate ratios (RRs) or hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs.The prespecified primary outcome was the composite of all-cause mortality and recurrent cardiovascular events. Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality, cardiovascular death, time to first primary outcome, functional capacity (6-minute walk distance), and health status (Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire-Overall Summary Score).A total of 2 studies (HELIOS-B and CARDIO-TTRansform) met the inclusion criteria and included 2086 patients with ATTR-CM. The studies included 1902 men with a median age of 77 years (range for HELIOS-B, 45-85 years; for CARDIO-TTRansform, 41-91 years). Gene-silencing therapy reduced the primary end point by 20% (RR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.69-0.94; P = .006), with no heterogeneity between trials (P for heterogeneity = .28). Gene-silencing therapy also reduced the risk of all-cause death (HR, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.61-0.91) and time to first all-cause death or cardiovascular events (HR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.67-0.89) compared with placebo. Gene silencers preserved 6-minute walk distance (placebo-corrected difference, +22.2 m; 95% CI, 14.3-30.0) and Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire-Overall Summary Score (+4.5; 95% CI, 2.7-6.2), with no evidence of between-trial heterogeneity. Treatment effects on primary end points differed according to baseline stabilizer use, with significant benefits observed among patients not receiving background stabilizer therapy (RR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.57-0.85) and no significant incremental benefit observed for those receiving concomitant stabilizer at baseline (RR, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.77-1.23; P for heterogeneity = .03). Similar heterogeneity was observed for functional capacity and health status.The findings from this meta-analysis support TTR gene silencing for ATTR-CM. The attenuated benefit observed for patients receiving concomitant TTR stabilizer therapy may reflect residual differences in case mix, disease duration, or magnitude of TTR suppression or a true ceiling on additional benefit of gene silencing in the setting of background TTR stabilization.PROSPERO registration: CRD420261421656. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether gene-silencing therapies, which reduce the production of a harmful protein in the liver called transthyretin, could help patients with a serious heart condition caused by this protein buildup. The team combined results from two large clinical trials involving over two thousand patients to compare how well gene-silencing therapy worked compared to a placebo, or fake treatment. Gene-silencing therapy reduced the risk of death and heart problems by twenty percent and also helped patients maintain their ability to walk and improved their quality of life compared to those receiving placebo. The treatment worked much better for patients who were not already taking other medications to stabilize the harmful protein, suggesting that combining gene-silencing therapy with existing treatments may not provide additional benefits. These findings support using gene-silencing therapy to treat this type of heart disease, though doctors may need to consider which patients will benefit most based on what other medications they are already taking.

title: 124I-Evuzamitide Positron Emission Tomography/Computed Tomography for Diagnosing Cardiac Amyloidosis: The REVEAL Nonrandomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: Diagnosing cardiac amyloidosis remains challenging because current imaging approaches are limited to transthyretin amyloidosis. A noninvasive test capable of directly imaging cardiac amyloidosis from various amyloid types and in multiple organs could address an important unmet diagnostic need.To evaluate the sensitivity and specificity of 124I-evuzamitide positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) for diagnosing cardiac amyloidosis.Prospective, multicenter (18 US centers), single-group study evaluating the efficacy of 124I-evuzamitide to diagnose cardiac amyloidosis. This study was conducted from January 14, 2025, to March 12, 2026, including a 60-day follow-up period. Three physicians with cardiac PET/CT experience independently reviewed PET/CT images for visual cardiac 124I-evuzamitide uptake while blinded to clinical data. Three expert clinical amyloidosis physicians, blinded to PET/CT data, independently adjudicated the diagnosis based on the standard-of-care diagnostic algorithm. A total of 195 adults suspected of having cardiac amyloidosis were enrolled when they presented for diagnostic evaluation at participating institutions, excluding patients with an established diagnosis of cardiac or systemic amyloidosis.PET/CT scans were obtained 3 to 5 hours after intravenous administration of 1 mCi of 124I-evuzamitide. Potassium iodide (130 mg) was given orally for 3 days starting at least 30 minutes prior to 124I-evuzamitide injection.Coprimary end points of this study were to assess the sensitivity and specificity of 124I-evuzamitide for the diagnosis of cardiac amyloidosis.Overall, 170 patients were included (median [IQR] age, 72 [64-79] years; 75.3% male, 19.2% Black, 79.0% White). Median N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide was 471 pg/mL and 61.7% had New York Heart Association class II or III heart failure symptoms. The overall sensitivity was 94% (95% CI, 85%-98%; P < .001); specificity, 86% (95% CI, 77%-92%; P < .001); positive predictive value, 85% (95% CI, 75%-92%); and negative predictive value, 94% (95% CI, 87%-98%).124I-evuzamitide PET/CT is highly sensitive and specific for diagnosing cardiac amyloidosis with an acceptable safety profile. These results support 124I-evuzamitide PET/CT as a diagnostic test to evaluate patients with suspected cardiac amyloidosis.ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06788535.

llm_summary: Diagnosing heart disease caused by amyloid protein buildup has been difficult because existing imaging tests only work for certain types of amyloid, creating a real need for better diagnostic tools. Researchers tested a new imaging scan called 124I-evuzamitide positron emission tomography, which uses a radioactive tracer to directly detect amyloid deposits in the heart, across eighteen medical centers in the United States with 170 patients suspected of having this condition. The new imaging test successfully identified cardiac amyloidosis in 94 percent of patients who actually had the disease and correctly ruled it out in 86 percent of patients who did not have it, with results that were statistically significant and reliable. These findings suggest that 124I-evuzamitide imaging could become an important new tool for doctors to diagnose cardiac amyloidosis more accurately and earlier, potentially improving patient care and treatment decisions. The study had an acceptable safety profile, though further research and real-world use will be needed to confirm these promising results and determine how this test fits into standard medical practice.

title: Pharmacologic Treatment for Migraine Prevention in Adults Practice Guideline Recommendations: Report of the AAN Guidelines Subcommittee and the American Headache Society.
abstract: This practice guideline provides updated evidence-based recommendations regarding the use of pharmacologic migraine prevention in adults. A multidisciplinary panel conducted a systematic review and developed practice recommendations following the process outlined in the 2017 edition of the American Academy of Neurology Clinical Practice Guideline Process Manual. The systematic review includes studies published through June 6, 2024, and is available in a companion publication. Recommendations are supported by structured rationales that integrate evidence from the systematic review, related evidence, principles of care, and inferences from evidence. Recommendations are provided on how to decide when it is appropriate to start a pharmacologic migraine preventive medication and how to decide which migraine preventive medication to start. Recommendations address decision making on appropriate choices of migraine preventive medications in specific situations and populations, including patients with fibromyalgia, obesity, or hypertension; considerations for older adults; treatment during pregnancy and lactation; sex-related factors in choosing medications; and treatment for patients with medication overuse. Recommendations on assessment of treatment efficacy, adverse effects, and discontinuing migraine preventive medications are provided.

llm_summary: A team of headache specialists and neurologists created updated guidelines to help doctors choose the best medications for preventing migraines in adults, since migraine is a common and disabling condition that affects millions of people. The researchers reviewed all scientific studies published through June 2024 and used a systematic process to develop clear recommendations about when patients should start preventive medications and which drugs work best for different situations. The guidelines cover specific advice for patients with other health conditions like fibromyalgia or high blood pressure, special considerations for pregnant women and older adults, and guidance on how to handle medication overuse and side effects. These recommendations give doctors practical tools to make better decisions about migraine prevention tailored to each patient's unique circumstances and health needs. The guidelines represent the most current evidence available and should help improve how doctors treat and manage migraines in their adult patients.

title: Systematic Review of Pharmacologic Treatment for Migraine Prevention in Adults: Report of the AAN Guidelines Subcommittee and the American Headache Society.
abstract: This systematic review (SR) provides updated evidence-based conclusions regarding the use of pharmacologic migraine prevention in adults to inform a new joint American Academy of Neurology (AAN) and American Headache Society practice guideline.A multidisciplinary panel conducted an SR following the 2017 AAN Clinical Practice Guideline Process Manual. Randomized controlled trials evaluating pharmacologic preventive treatments for adults with episodic or chronic migraine were included. Searches encompassed MEDLINE, Embase, and ClinicalTrials.gov from database inception through June 6, 2024. Studies were screened in duplicate, with dual independent risk-of-bias assessment. Outcomes included change in monthly headache days, ≥50% responder rate, and validated patient-reported quality of life (QOL) measures. Raw mean differences, standardized mean differences, and risk ratios were calculated. A modified Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation process was used to classify certainty of evidence.A total of 217 studies met inclusion criteria. For episodic migraine, high-confidence evidence showed that galcanezumab and erenumab are more effective than placebo in reducing headache frequency. Moderate-confidence evidence supported benefit from atogepant, eptinezumab, fremanezumab, propranolol, topiramate, and valproate. Several additional oral agents including amitriptyline, bisoprolol, flunarizine, fluoxetine, levetiracetam, metoprolol, nifedipine, pizotifen, and telmisartan had low-confidence evidence suggesting possible benefit. For chronic migraine, high-confidence evidence supported reductions in headache frequency with fremanezumab, galcanezumab, and onabotulinumtoxinA. Moderate-confidence evidence supported benefit from atogepant, eptinezumab, erenumab, topiramate and valproate. Across both episodic and chronic migraine populations, erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab, rimegepant, atogepant, topiramate and onabotulinumtoxinA demonstrated improvements in patient-reported QOL outcomes on validated instruments. Evidence comparing active treatments was limited and generally of low or very low confidence, restricting conclusions about comparative effectiveness.This SR provides a comprehensive synthesis of evidence on pharmacologic migraine prevention in adults. High- and moderate-confidence findings confirm the efficacy of several established and newer preventive therapies and demonstrate improvements in patient-reported outcomes across multiple validated measures. These conclusions informed the development of evidence-based recommendations, presented in a companion publication, to guide clinicians in selecting preventive medications for adults with episodic and chronic migraine.

llm_summary: Migraine is a common and disabling condition that affects many adults, making it important to find effective medications that can prevent these severe headaches from occurring in the first place. Researchers conducted a comprehensive review of 217 scientific studies that tested different preventive medications in adults with either occasional migraines or chronic migraines that happen frequently throughout the month. The review found strong evidence that certain newer injectable medications like galcanezumab and erenumab work better than placebo (a fake treatment) at reducing how often migraines occur, while older medications like topiramate and propranolol also showed moderate evidence of benefit. Several medications including newer oral drugs and botulinum toxin injections also improved patients' quality of life by reducing pain and disability related to their migraines. This comprehensive summary of available evidence will help doctors choose the most effective migraine prevention medications for their individual patients based on what scientific research shows actually works.

title: Response-predictive MRI biomarkers of low-dose lithium therapy: cortical thickness changes in patients with bipolar depression.
abstract: Lithium remains a cornerstone treatment for bipolar disorder, yet response rates are variable and predicting outcomes remains challenging. This study examined whether cortical thickness changes during lithium treatment serve and their association with clinical outcomes in bipolar depression, aiming to characterize the neurobiological correlates of treatment response.Twenty-three adult outpatients (17 female, 6 male; 74% bipolar II; mean age 28.5 years), medication-free and treatment-naïve, received six-week low-therapeutic lithium monotherapy (mean level 0.47±0.19 mmol/L). Cortical thickness was assessed via 3T MRI across 68 regions using multivariate Bayesian GLMMs controlling for age, sex, and subtype.Forty-two of 68 regions showed moderate-to-strong evidence for cortical change. Increased thickness in right rostral anterior cingulate, right isthmus cingulate, right lateral orbitofrontal cortex, and right frontal pole were associated with remission. Remitters showed decreased prefrontal-cingulate thickness but increased visual-temporal thickness, suggesting localized neuroplastic effects specific to lithium response.Regional cortical thickness changes during lithium treatment represent promising neurobiological correlates of therapeutic response in bipolar depression, advancing understanding of the pathways underlying lithium's effects. Future studies should validate these findings in larger, prospective cohorts to assess their potential translational relevance.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Lithium is a long-standing medication for bipolar disorder, a serious mental health condition marked by extreme mood swings, but doctors struggle to predict which patients will benefit from treatment. Researchers studied twenty-three adults with bipolar depression who had never taken psychiatric medication before, giving them low doses of lithium for six weeks while using brain imaging scans to measure changes in the thickness of their brain's outer layer. The results showed that patients whose symptoms improved had specific patterns of brain changes, including thickening in certain areas involved in emotion regulation and decision-making, while other brain regions showed thinning. These findings suggest that measuring brain thickness changes during early lithium treatment could potentially help doctors identify which patients will respond well to the medication before waiting weeks to see if symptoms improve. Future research with larger groups of patients will be needed to confirm these results and determine whether brain imaging could become a practical tool for predicting treatment success in bipolar depression.

title: MRI multicomponent relaxometry for liver fibrosis, inflammation, and steatosis in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis: A prospective study.
abstract: To validate contrast-free MRI multicomponent relaxometry (MCR) for noninvasive quantification of fibrosis, inflammation, steatosis, and iron in biopsy-proven metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), formerly nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).In this prospective single-center study, adults with biopsy-confirmed MASH underwent MRI within 6 months of biopsy; healthy volunteers served as controls. The 10-minute protocol comprised multi-echo gradient-echo (for proton density fat fraction, PDFF, and R2*w) and multi-echo spin-echo (for MCR). Histopathology served as the reference (fibrosis, ballooning, lobular inflammation, steatosis, iron) read blinded to imaging. The primary biomarker was extracellular non-vascular water fraction (ECNVwf).Spearman correlations (rs); receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis with area under the ROC (AUROC); bootstrap validation (1000 replicates); interobserver agreement by intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC).122 participants: 106 MASH patients (68 women, 38 men; mean age 50.5 ± 11.4 years) and 16 controls (7 women, 9 men; 33.6 ± 6.2 years). ECNVwf correlated with fibrosis (rs = 0.80; p < 0.001) and detected any fibrosis (F1-F4 vs F0) with AUROC 0.94 (threshold 14.65%; specificity 100%; sensitivity 85%; bootstrap 95% CI: 14.2-14.7%; ordinal AUROC: 0.87). ECNVwf correlated with ballooning (rs = 0.65; p < 0.001; AUROC 0.92) and inflammation (rs = 0.52; p < 0.001; AUROC 0.94). PDFF correlated with steatosis (rs = 0.72; AUROC 0.96), and R2*w with iron (rs = 0.52; AUROC 0.97). Interobserver agreement was excellent (ICC: ECNVwf 0.973; R2*w 0.979; PDFF 0.994).Contrast-free MCR enables accurate detection of fibrosis and comprehensive characterization of inflammation, fat, and iron in MASH, warranting further multicenter studies.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a new type of MRI scan without contrast dye could detect liver damage from a condition called metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, which involves fat buildup, inflammation, and scarring in the liver. The study involved 106 patients with confirmed liver disease and 16 healthy volunteers who underwent a ten-minute MRI scan that measured different properties of liver tissue, and doctors compared these measurements to actual tissue samples taken from biopsies. The MRI scan successfully detected liver scarring with very high accuracy, correctly identifying 85 percent of patients with scarring while having zero false alarms, and it also accurately measured fat content, inflammation, and iron levels in the liver. These results suggest that this new scanning method could replace the need for painful liver biopsies in the future, allowing doctors to monitor liver disease more easily and help patients avoid invasive procedures. The researchers recommend that larger studies at multiple medical centers be conducted to confirm these findings before this scanning technique becomes standard practice in hospitals.

title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging Artifact Associated With the Oticon Medical Sentio Ti Transcutaneous Bone Conduction Hearing Implant.
abstract: To evaluate magnetic resonance (MR) imaging artifact and image distortion associated with the Oticon Medical Sentio Ti bone conduction implant (BCI) and identify optimized imaging techniques.Cadaveric study.One cadaveric head specimen was unilaterally implanted with Sentio Ti BCI according to the manufacturer's instructions.Imaging was performed with a Siemens 1.5 Tesla MR machine on XA60 software before and after implantation. Imaging was performed with both standard and metal mitigation techniques. Image scoring (diagnostic vs. nondiagnostic) and qualitative assessment of anatomic subsites were performed by 2 experienced neuroradiologists.Image distortion and artifact were noted in all postimplant sequences. For all sequences, imaging of the ipsilateral middle ear, mastoid, and internal auditory canal (IAC) was nondiagnostic. The axial T1 turbo spin echo high bandwidth sequence had the best artifact reduction; however, the ipsilateral temporal bone remained nondiagnostic. Notably, nonecho planar diffusion-weighted imaging (non-EPI DWI) was nondiagnostic for both the ipsilateral temporal bone and the contralateral IAC and middle ear.After implantation of the Sentio Ti BCI, imaging of the ipsilateral temporal bone is rendered nondiagnostic on all MR sequences due to artifact despite the use of metal mitigation techniques. Importantly, the non-EPI DWI HASTE sequence, which is used for cholesteatoma surveillance, is nondiagnostic for all ipsilateral and most contralateral temporal bone subsites, making cholesteatoma surveillance challenging with an implant in place. This finding is critical for clinical decision-making, as rehabilitation of conductive hearing loss in the setting of chronic otitis media is among the most common indications for use of a BCI.Copyright © 2026, Otology & Neurotology, Inc.

llm_summary: Researchers examined how a bone conduction hearing implant called the Sentio Ti affects magnetic resonance imaging, which is a scanning technology doctors use to see inside the body. They implanted this device in one cadaver head and performed MRI scans before and after the implant was placed to compare the image quality. The results showed that the metal in the implant created significant distortion and artifacts, or blurry spots, that made images of the ear bone on the implanted side impossible to read clearly, even when doctors used special techniques designed to reduce metal-related problems. This finding is especially concerning because one particular type of scan used to check for a serious ear condition called cholesteatoma became unreadable on both the implanted side and parts of the other side. The study highlights an important challenge for patients who receive this hearing implant, since many people get it to treat hearing loss related to chronic ear infections, and doctors may struggle to monitor their ears for complications after surgery.

title: Machine Learning in Postcardiotomy Shock: Implications for Temporary Mechanical Circulatory Support.
abstract: Postcardiotomy shock (PCS) is a distinct form of cardiogenic shock that occurs after cardiac surgery and necessitates rapid decisions regarding temporary mechanical circulatory support (tMCS), including escalation, device configuration, and weaning. Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a strategy to integrate high-dimensional perioperative data and augment clinical decision-making beyond traditional risk scores. This narrative expert review evaluates ML applications across the PCS continuum, including early risk recognition and phenotyping, tMCS initiation, management and liberation, and prognostication. This study also summarizes key aspects of ML model development, including feature selection, outcome definition, external validation, and clinical implementation. Current evidence is strongest for risk stratification, mortality prediction, and weaning support, particularly in venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation cohorts. However, most models are retrospective, derived from heterogeneous shock populations, and lack prospective validation in PCS-specific cohorts. Emerging work on automated device titration is promising but remains preclinical. ML should be considered an adjunct to clinician judgment rather than a substitute for it. Future progress will depend on high-quality PCS datasets, prospective validation, seamless workflow integration, and governance frameworks that ensure safe, transparent, and equitable implementation.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Postcardiotomy shock, a serious heart condition that develops after heart surgery and requires quick decisions about temporary mechanical support devices, is difficult to manage using traditional prediction methods alone. Researchers reviewed how machine learning, a type of artificial intelligence that learns patterns from large amounts of medical data, could help doctors make better decisions about when to use these support devices, how to adjust them, and when patients are ready to stop using them. The evidence shows that machine learning works best for predicting which patients will survive and for helping doctors decide when to remove support devices, especially in patients using a type of heart-lung machine called venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. However, most of the studies reviewed were based on past patient records rather than new patients being treated now, and they included patients with different types of shock rather than focusing only on postcardiotomy shock. To move forward, doctors and researchers need to collect better quality data specifically from postcardiotomy shock patients, test these artificial intelligence tools in real clinical settings, and create clear rules to ensure these tools are used safely and fairly alongside doctor judgment rather than replacing it.

title: Effectiveness and mechanistic effects of green mamba related peptide MQ232 in an orthologous mouse model of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
abstract: Tolvaptan, a vasopressin V2 receptor (V2R) inverse agonist, is the only treatment specifically approved for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). In addition to inhibiting cAMP synthesis, it has other effects on V2R signaling. Our goal was to mechanistically characterize the effects of MQ232, an optimized peptide of the green mamba snake and a new V2R inverse agonist, in Pkd1RC/RC mice.Pkd1RC/RC mice were treated with MQ232 (0.5, 2, 4, or 8 nmols/kg/hour via minipump), tolvaptan (0.2% in chow), or vehicle from four to 16 weeks of age. MRI measurements of kidney volume were used for randomization and endpoint, urine was collected at 12 and 16 weeks, and mice were sacrificed at 16 weeks for blood and tissue collections.MQ232 and tolvaptan equally attenuated PKD. In male mice, increasing doses of MQ232 were associated with greater reductions in kidney cAMP, aquaporin-2 expression and phosphorylation, and with higher urine outputs, but equally ameliorated PKD; there was no correlation between kidney cAMP or urine output with disease attenuation. Phosphorylated/total ratios for Src, ERK, CRAF, Akt, RPS6, and Stat3 were, in general, lower in the treated mice, but this was less or reversed with increasing MQ232 doses. Analysis of previous studies with tolvaptan showed similar dose-dependent effects. This is consistent with these compounds being dual efficacy V2R ligands with inverse agonistic activity on Gαs/cAMP and, at high doses, activating β-arrestin-dependent or -independent Src and ERK signaling. Both compounds downregulated PAPPA. MQ232 inhibited IGF1Rβ phosphorylation, whereas tolvaptan at the dose/schedule used in the study did not.Vasopressin binding to V2R activates many cystogenic pathways: Gαs/cAMP, β-arrestin-Src and β-arrestin-ERK, and PAPPA and IGF1R signaling. Activation of cAMP-independent signaling may limit the benefit from MQ232 and tolvaptan when administered at high doses, questioning the rationale of titrating these compounds to maximally tolerated doses to treat ADPKD. Improved understanding of V2R signaling in ADPKD will lead to better therapies.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, a genetic condition where fluid-filled cysts grow in the kidneys and cause organ failure, currently has only one approved treatment called tolvaptan, which works by blocking a specific protein receptor involved in cyst formation. Researchers tested a new drug called MQ232, derived from green mamba snake venom and designed to work similarly to tolvaptan, in mice that naturally develop this kidney disease to understand how both drugs actually stop cyst growth. The study found that MQ232 and tolvaptan were equally effective at slowing kidney cyst development, but surprisingly, higher doses of MQ232 did not improve results even though they reduced more of the chemical signals thought to cause the disease. The researchers discovered that both drugs work through multiple pathways in cells, and at high doses they may actually activate some of the same harmful signals they are supposed to block, which could explain why giving patients the maximum tolerated dose might not be the best approach. These findings suggest that future treatments for polycystic kidney disease should be carefully designed to target the right cellular pathways without accidentally triggering cyst-promoting signals, and doctors may need to.

title: Microsurgical treatment of lower extremity lymphedema: An umbrella systematic review supporting the American Venous Forum and the American Vein and Lymphatic Society clinical practice guidelines on management of lymphedema.
abstract: Lymphovenous anastomosis (LVA) and vascularized lymph node transfer (VLNT) are established microsurgical options for chronic lymphedema. This umbrella systematic review synthesizes evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses to define indications for lymphatic microsurgery and inform forthcoming practice guidelines of the American Venous Forum and the American Vein and Lymphatic Society.A systematic search of multiple electronic databases identified English-language systematic reviews and meta-analyses published between 2010 and 2025 addressing microsurgical treatment or prevention of lower-extremity lymphedema (LEL). Eligible studies reported objective and/or patient-reported outcomes and addressed clinical questions prioritized by the American Venous Forum/the American Vein and Lymphatic Society Guideline Committee.Twenty-six systematic reviews, including 14 meta-analyses, were analyzed; no randomized controlled trials were identified. Twenty reviews evaluated treatment of LEL; 16 also included upper-extremity lymphedema. Six assessed immediate lymphatic reconstruction (ILR) following tumor excision with inguinal lymphadenectomy. Conclusions were primarily driven by four moderate-quality treatment reviews and one high-quality prevention review that satisfied all critical A MeaSurement Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews 2 domains. Due to substantial overlap of primary studies across reviews, findings were synthesized qualitatively, and effect estimates were not pooled to avoid double counting. Both LVA and VLNT were effective. LVA was more commonly performed in earlier disease stages. Limb volume/circumference reduction ranged from 34.16% [95% confidence interval (CI), 23.93-44.40] to 46.8% (95% CI, 43.2-50.4), with follow-up from 1 month to 8 years (Evidence C, low- to very-low quality). Postoperative cellulitis, reported in 12 reviews, decreased by 2.1 episodes/year after VLNT (95% CI, -2.7 to -1.4) and from an annual incidence of 0.84 to 0.07 following LVA (Evidence B, moderate quality). Symptoms or quality of life improved in 50% to 100% of patients across 17 reviews. No deaths or major complications were reported; minor complications were more frequent after VLNT. ILR reduced the risk of LEL by 30.3 per 100 patients treated compared with no ILR (risk difference, -30.3%; 95% CI, -46.5% to -14%; P<.001). Low-quality evidence from one review suggested possible association between ILR and worse oncologic outcomes in lower-extremity melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma.Evidence supports LVA for both primary and secondary LEL when functional lymphatic channels are identified, irrespective of disease stage. VLNT may provide greater benefit in advanced disease but is associated with higher morbidity. ILR is supported for the prevention of LEL following pelvic or truncal oncologic surgery with iliofemoral lymphadenectomy but should likely be avoided in extremity dermatologic malignancies. Guideline recommendations should emphasize shared decision-making and incorporate patient preferences, procedural cost, available technology, and surgeon expertise.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Researchers examined evidence from multiple systematic reviews to understand how two types of microsurgery, which are precise surgical techniques using magnification, can help people with lymphedema, a condition where fluid builds up in the legs and causes swelling. The team looked at studies published between 2010 and 2025 that tested two main surgical approaches: connecting lymph vessels directly together or transplanting healthy lymph nodes from other parts of the body to restore proper fluid drainage. Both surgical approaches were found to reduce limb swelling by about one-third to one-half, decrease painful skin infections from multiple times per year to almost never, and improve quality of life for most patients, with few serious complications reported. The surgery that connects vessels directly worked well for people in earlier disease stages, while transplanting lymph nodes appeared more helpful for people with advanced swelling, though it carried a higher risk of minor side effects. These findings support using these microsurgical techniques for treating leg lymphedema, but doctors should discuss with patients which approach fits best based on disease severity, cost, available technology, and the surgeon's experience.

title: Rating certainty of evidence when the target threshold is a value-based threshold and the point estimate is close to that threshold.
abstract: It is crucial, when using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE), that authors are clear about what it is in which they are rating the certainty of evidence (ie, the target of certainty of evidence rating). This article addresses challenges GRADE users face in choosing a target of certainty rating for any value-based threshold (ie, little or no difference; an important effect; small, moderate or large difference) when the point estimate is close to that threshold.Using an iterative process, authors generated and refined possible solutions to the identified challenges.The challenges GRADE users face when point estimates prove close to the initially chosen value-based threshold include (1) the intuitive interpretation of the point estimate is similar whichever side of the threshold the point estimate lies on but the formal interpretation differs greatly and (2) rating down for imprecision due to the confidence interval (CI) crossing the threshold when the CI is very narrow. This paper provides four possible solutions. The first is continuing to rate certainty in an important or unimportant effect and rating down for imprecision when the CI crosses the MID. The second is to consider uncertainty around the MID, rating certainty in relation to a range of plausible MIDs (ie, a range formed by the smallest plausible MID and the largest plausible MID), and rate down for imprecision when the CI crosses either plausibility bound. The third solution is considering both the null and moderate effect thresholds, rating certainty in a trivial or small effect, and rating down for imprecision when the CI crosses either threshold. The fourth solution is using more than one of the above solutions and presenting two or more certainty of evidence ratings.GRADE users should note these challenges and apply their chosen solution to transparently determine the target of their certainty rating.When point estimates prove to be close to the initially chosen value-based threshold, to decide on what it is in which GRADE users rate their certainty (ie, the target of certainty rating), GRADE users face challenges. This paper provides four possible solutions related to the minimal important difference (MID) that are also applicable to other value-based thresholds. llm_summary: When doctors and researchers evaluate medical evidence to make treatment recommendations, they use a system called GRADE that rates how confident they can be in their findings, but this system faces challenges when study results fall very close to the threshold that separates an important treatment effect from an unimportant one. Researchers worked through an iterative process, meaning they repeatedly tested and refined possible solutions, to identify and address the specific problems that occur when a point estimate (the main result from a study) lands near a value-based threshold like the minimal important difference, which is the smallest change in health that patients would actually notice. The team discovered two main challenges: first, when results hover near the threshold, the intuitive meaning seems similar regardless of which side of the line the result falls on, yet the formal interpretation changes dramatically, and second, researchers may incorrectly downgrade their confidence rating simply because the confidence interval (the range of likely true values) crosses the threshold, even when that interval is very narrow. The authors proposed four possible solutions that GRADE users can apply, including continuing with the original approach but being more careful about imprecision, considering a range of plausible thresholds instead of just one fixed number, evaluating.

title: IN.PACT AV Access Post-Approval Study of a Paclitaxel Drug-Coated Balloon for the Treatment of Dysfunctional Arteriovenous Dialysis Circuits.
abstract: To report the 12-month safety and effectiveness data of a drug-coated balloon (DCB) for the treatment of de novo or restenotic (nonstented) lesions in native arteriovenous fistulae (AVFs) in patients requiring hemodialysis.The IN.PACT AV Post-Approval Study is a prospective, multicenter, single-arm study conducted in the United States. In the primary cohort, 159 eligible participants (163 lesions) received DCB treatment at 15 sites and are included in this analysis. The primary endpoint was the serious infection rate through 12 months, including pneumonia but excluding coronavirus disease 2019, relative to a 30% performance goal. The secondary endpoint was 12-month mortality. Ancillary endpoints included, but were not limited to, target lesion primary patency (TLPP), access circuit primary patency (ACPP), and reinterventions through 24 months. An angiographic core laboratory adjudicated reinterventions and an independent Clinical Events Committee adjudicated events.The study met the primary endpoint with a serious infection rate of 13.4% (95% CI, 8.9%-20.1%) through 12 months. All-cause mortality was 19.4% (14.0%-26.5%). TLPP and ACPP through 12 months were 70.2% (61.8%-77.1%) and 52.6% (44.0%-60.5%), respectively. Means of 0.6 (± 1.0 SD) and 0.7 (± 1.1 SD) interventions were required within 12 months to maintain target lesion patency and access circuit patency, respectively, with a target lesion revascularization rate of 38.9% (31.4%-47.5%).The primary endpoint was met with a low serious infection rate. The TLPP and ACPP outcomes showed the durability of DCB treatment for AVFs. Results support the safety and effectiveness of paclitaxel DCBs for treating de novo and restenotic AVF lesions.Copyright © 2026 SIR. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

The study followed 159 patients across 15 medical centers in the United States who received this drug-coated balloon treatment, and doctors tracked their health for one year to measure infection rates, death rates, and how long the blood vessels stayed open. The treatment successfully met its main safety goal by keeping the serious infection rate low at about 13 percent, and about 70 percent of the treated blood vessels remained open and working after 12 months. The results show that this drug-coated balloon approach is both safe and effective for treating blocked dialysis access points, which is important because keeping these blood vessels open helps dialysis patients receive the treatment they need. While the study demonstrates promising outcomes, patients did need additional procedures about once every two months on average to maintain the blood vessel openings, suggesting that ongoing monitoring and care remain necessary.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists and post-endovascular thrombectomy outcomes in acute ischemic stroke: a multicenter propensity score matched analysis.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1As) have demonstrated cardiovascular and cerebrovascular benefits in high-risk populations, but their impact in patients with acute ischemic stroke (AIS) requiring endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) remains uncertain.We performed a retrospective cohort analysis using the TriNetX Network, identifying adults (≥18 years) with AIS treated with EVT from January 1, 2016 through December 31, 2025. Patients with GLP-1A exposure within three months prior to EVT constituted the exposure cohort; those without served as comparators. This pre-index window was specified to eliminate immortal time bias, with follow-up beginning on the EVT date for both cohorts. Three-year outcomes included all-cause mortality and inpatient hospitalizations. One-to-one propensity score matching was applied using demographic, comorbidity, medication, and metabolic variables including individual National Institute of Health Stroke Scale scores, Hemoglobin A1c, and body mass index.Among 286 GLP-1A-exposed and 19,263 unexposed EVT-treated patients, 261 matched pairs were analyzed. GLP-1A use was associated with lower all-cause mortality (11.5% vs 29.9%; HR 0.334, 95% CI 0.219-0.508) and fewer inpatient hospitalizations (39.8% vs 54.8%; HR 0.514, 95% CI 0.398-0.663), both p < 0.001.Among EVT-treated AIS patients, GLP-1A exposure within three months prior to EVT was associated with improved survival and reduced inpatient hospitalizations.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: The evolving role of artificial intelligence in ophthalmology: basic science, translation, and clinical integration.
abstract: Ophthalmology has emerged as the proving ground for medical artificial intelligence (AI) because of its imaging-centric workflows, standardized data acquisition, and well defined clinical endpoints. Recently, the field has started transitioning from narrowly trained, task-specific algorithms toward multimodal models that are trained on large datasets and can be adapted to many tasks. These models may integrate information from images, text, and clinical data and are increasingly trialed in real-world settings. This review examines recent advances and ongoing controversies in the use of AI as a basic science, translational, and clinical research tool in ophthalmology.Recent literature highlights the growing role of self-supervised and foundation models for scalable phenotyping, biomarker discovery, and cross-task generalization, particularly in retinal imaging and optical coherence tomography (OCT). In parallel, large-scale clinical deployments, including cloud-based OCT platforms and autonomous diabetic retinopathy screening, demonstrate clinical impact while revealing persistent challenges related to workflow integration and patient generalizability. Regulatory and ethics-focused studies underscore increasing attention to validation rigor, bias, and postdeployment monitoring, exposing heterogeneity in research standards and physician practices.Ophthalmic AI is maturing toward real-world clinical implementation. Future progress will depend less on performance gains alone and more on clinical alignment, rigorous validation, equity-aware evaluation, and postdeployment surveillance, alongside continued investment in basic science to advance disease understanding and inform robust, generalizable model development.Copyright © 2026 Wolters Kluwer Health, LLC. llm_summary: Ophthalmology, which is the medical field focused on eye care, has become a leading area for testing artificial intelligence because eye doctors rely heavily on images and have clear ways to measure whether treatments work. Researchers reviewed recent advances in how artificial intelligence is being used in eye care, noting a shift from simple programs designed for one specific task toward more complex systems trained on large amounts of data that can handle many different jobs at once. These newer artificial intelligence systems are now being tested in real hospitals and clinics, where they help doctors discover new disease patterns in retinal images and eye scans while also screening patients for conditions like diabetic retinopathy, which is vision damage caused by diabetes. However, the research also revealed important challenges that need to be solved before these tools can be widely used, including making sure the systems work fairly for all patients, integrating them smoothly into doctor's daily routines, and continuing to monitor how well they perform after they are deployed in hospitals. Moving forward, the success of artificial intelligence in eye care will depend not just on making the technology more accurate but also on ensuring it is thoroughly tested, works fairly across different patient populations, and is carefully watched over time to catch any problems.

title: COMPARING REFRACTIVE OUTCOMES OF SECONDARY LENS SURGERY BETWEEN OPHTHALMOLOGY SUBSPECIALTIES IN PATIENTS WITH GOOD FINAL VISION.
abstract: The study compares refractive outcomes of secondary intraocular lens (SIOL) surgery performed by vitreoretinal, anterior segment, and both surgeons.Eyes included in this study underwent SIOL surgery from 2012 to 2024 and had a final postoperative visual acuity of 20/50 or better. Regression analysis compared refractive outcomes, and chi-squared analysis compared complications between subspecialty of SIOL surgeons.A total of 94, 104, and 80 eyes were included in the retina surgeon, anterior segment surgeon, and combo surgeon cohorts, respectively. There was no significant difference in error between target and final postoperative spherical equivalence between retina and combo ( P = 0.079), retina and anterior segment ( P = 0.135), or anterior segment and combo cohorts ( P = 0.567). There was no significant difference in number of eyes with final spherical equivalence within 1 diopter of target spherical equivalence between retina and combo ( P = 0.136), retina and anterior segment ( P = 0.061), or anterior segment and combo cohorts ( P = 0.783). The retina cohort had higher postoperative corneal edema than the combo ( P = 0.017) and the anterior segment cohorts ( P = 0.035). The combo cohort had more postoperative retinal detachment than the anterior segment cohort ( P = 0.046).In eyes with good final vision, retina and anterior segment surgeons have similar refractive outcomes after SIOL surgery.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether the type of eye surgeon performing secondary lens implant surgery, which is a procedure to correct vision problems after cataract surgery, affects how well the final vision turns out. The study included 278 patients who had this secondary lens surgery between 2012 and 2024, divided into three groups based on whether a retina specialist, cornea and front-of-eye specialist, or both types of surgeons performed the procedure. All patients ended up with good final vision of 20/50 or better, and the researchers compared how accurately each surgeon type achieved the target vision prescription and whether complications occurred. The results showed that retina surgeons and front-of-eye surgeons achieved nearly identical refractive outcomes, meaning they were equally successful at getting patients to their desired vision prescription. However, retina surgeons had more cases of corneal swelling after surgery, while surgeons trained in both specialties had slightly more cases of retinal detachment, suggesting that while vision outcomes are similar, different surgeon types may experience different types of complications.

title: Long-Term Outcomes of Paroxysmal and Persistent Atrial Fibrillation Management Strategy During Nonemergent Coronary Artery Bypass Surgery.
abstract: Management of atrial fibrillation (AF) at the time of coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) is a class 1 recommendation. This study evaluated trends in AF management and their association with long-term survival.Patients with paroxysmal or persistent AF who underwent isolated CABG were identified from The Society of Thoracic Surgeons Adult Cardiac Surgery Database (2011-2022) with linkage to Medicare claims for long-term outcomes. Patients were stratified by AF treatment: none, left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) only, epicardial ablation (EA), or intracardiac ablation (IA). The primary end point was all-cause mortality; secondary end points included permanent pacemaker placement, stroke, and readmission for AF, bleeding, or heart failure. Long-term mortality was assessed using Kaplan-Meier methods and Cox regression. Nonfatal outcomes were assessed using competing-risk regression with death as the competing event.Among 59,331 patients, 71.0% had paroxysmal AF, increasing from 56.6% (2011) to 79.6% (2022). AF treatment included none (51.0%), LAAO only (15.3%), EA (25.4%), and IA (8.2%). AF treatment increased from 31.8% to 68.8%, driven by LAAO (1.2%-30.8%). Patients with persistent AF had higher mortality than patients with paroxysmal AF (P < .001). EA showed lower mortality compared with no treatment. IA was associated with higher pacemaker implantation (6.0% vs 3.2%-3.4% in other groups; P < .001). Compared with no treatment, all treatment groups had lower stroke risk (subdistribution hazard ratio, 0.64-0.79; P < .001) and lower AF readmission (subdistribution hazard ratio, 0.85-0.89; P < .05).Nearly one-half of patients with AF who underwent CABG receive no treatment. Epicardial ablation was associated with superior long-term survival, and all strategies with were associated lower stroke risk.Copyright © 2026 The Society of Thoracic Surgeons. llm_summary: Researchers examined how doctors manage atrial fibrillation, a common heart rhythm problem, when patients undergo bypass surgery to improve blood flow to the heart. The study looked at nearly 60,000 patients from 2011 to 2022 and compared four different treatment approaches: doing nothing, blocking off a small pouch in the heart called the left atrial appendage, using heat or cold to scar heart tissue through the skin, or using electrical energy to scar tissue from inside the heart. The results showed that about half of patients with atrial fibrillation received no treatment at all, while the use of left atrial appendage blocking increased dramatically from just over one percent to nearly one-third of patients over the study period. Patients who received heat or cold scarring treatment had better long-term survival rates compared to those who received no treatment, and all treatment approaches reduced the risk of stroke and the need for hospital readmission related to heart rhythm problems. These findings suggest that treating atrial fibrillation during bypass surgery can improve patient outcomes, though doctors still need to determine which specific treatment works best for different types of patients.

llm_summary: Background:  Merkel cell carcinoma is a rare and aggressive type of skin cancer that often spreads to other parts of the body, making it difficult to treat and requiring advanced medical approaches. Immunotherapy, which is a type of cancer treatment that helps the body's immune system fight cancer cells, has become an important option for patients with this advanced form of the disease.

title: A survival analysis evaluating predictors of implant subsidence after one- or two-level anterior lumbar interbody fusion.
abstract: Anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) affords significant sagittal alignment, but overly aggressive correction carries the risk of interbody subsidence. We analyzed predictors of subsidence following ALIF.Patients who underwent 1- or 2-level ALIF were identified and data were collected on demographics, bone quality (assessed with Hounsfield units/HU), surgical characteristics, and radiographic parameters, including intradiscal lordosis angle (IDL) and disc height (DH). Cox regression was used to identify predictors of interbody subsidence ≥ 2 mm, significant subsidence (≥4mm), and loss of correction (ΔIDL ≥ 3°).252 patients (median 57 years; 51.2% male) operated at 335 unique levels were included; subsidence occurred in 29.6%, significant subsidence in 7.8%, and ΔIDL ≥ 3° in 18.5%. Subsidence on multivariable analysis was independently predicted by greater postoperative DH (HR 1.128/mm; [1.065, 1.196]; p < 0.001). Significant subsidence was predicted by greater BMI (HR 1.087 per kg/m2; [1.008, 1.173]; p = 0.031), lower HU in the cranial vertebra (HR 0.812 per 10HU; [0.717, 0.921]; p = 0.001), and greater postoperative disc height (HR 1.140/mm; [1.011, 1.287]; p = 0.033). Loss of correction was predicted by greater postoperative IDL (HR 1.097 per °; [1.046, 1.152]; p < 0.001). Implant dimensions nor compensation proved significant for any of the endpoints examined.Poorer bone quality and greater disc height restoration appear to predict both subsidence and significant subsidence following ALIF; increased BMI also predicts significant subsidence. Overly aggressive height restoration, especially in patients with weak bone, may increase the risk of subsidence and loss of correction.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Researchers examined what causes implants used in spine surgery to sink into the bone after anterior lumbar interbody fusion, a procedure where surgeons fuse vertebrae in the lower back by inserting a cage from the front of the body. The study followed 252 patients who had this surgery at one or two levels of the spine, collecting information about their age, weight, bone quality measured by special imaging, and how much the surgeons stretched open the disc space during surgery. The results showed that subsidence, or sinking of the implant, happened in about 30 percent of patients, and it was more likely to occur when surgeons created more disc height during the operation or when patients had weaker bone quality. The findings suggest that doctors should be careful not to stretch the disc space too aggressively during surgery, especially in patients with poor bone quality, because this increases the risk of the implant sinking and losing the correction that was achieved. Future research should focus on identifying which patients have weak bones before surgery so surgeons can adjust their approach and reduce complications.

title: Antidepressant therapy in the management of glioblastoma multiforme: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: To evaluate the association between antidepressant use and survival outcomes in patients with glioblastoma multiforme (GBM).A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. MEDLINE, Embase, and LILACS were searched for observational studies evaluating the association between antidepressant use and survival in patients with GBM. Hazard ratios (HRs) for overall survival were pooled using a random-effects model. Subgroup analyses were performed by antidepressant class, timing of initiation, and patient age. Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic, and meta-regression was conducted to explore potential sources of variability.Eight studies comprising 8915 patients were included. Antidepressant use was not significantly associated with overall survival (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.76-1.55; p = 0.64), with substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 95%). Subgroup analyses revealed no significant survival association when stratified by antidepressant class (SSRIs alone: HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.73-1.25; SSRIs and TCAs combined: HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.62-2.26), timing of initiation (pre-diagnosis: HR 0.91, 95% CI 0.63-1.32; post-diagnosis: HR 1.28, 95% CI 0.64-2.54), or age. Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis confirmed the robustness of the null finding. Meta-regression did not identify antidepressant exposure as a significant source of heterogeneity. Gross total resection was consistently associated with improved survival across studies.Current evidence does not support a survival benefit associated with antidepressant use in patients with GBM. Antidepressants should be prescribed based on psychiatric indications rather than with the expectation of oncological benefit. Prospective studies with standardized exposure definitions and molecular subtyping are needed to further clarify any potential therapeutic role.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether antidepressant medications, which are commonly prescribed to treat depression and anxiety, might also help improve survival outcomes in patients with glioblastoma multiforme, a highly aggressive type of brain cancer. The team conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis, which means they searched medical databases for eight previous studies involving nearly nine thousand patients and combined the results to look for patterns across all the research. The analysis found that taking antidepressants was not significantly associated with improved survival in glioblastoma patients, and this finding remained consistent whether researchers looked at different types of antidepressants, when the medications were started, or the age of the patients. Based on these results, doctors should prescribe antidepressants to glioblastoma patients only when they have depression or anxiety symptoms that need treatment, rather than hoping the medications will help fight the cancer itself. Future research using more rigorous study designs and better ways to track which patients took antidepressants and for how long would be needed to determine if there might be any hidden benefits that this current evidence did not reveal.

title: Neutrophil extracellular trap-related pathology in sporadic brain arteriovenous malformations after radiosurgery: An exploratory histopathological study.
abstract: Brain arteriovenous malformations (bAVMs) shunt arterial blood directly into veins, bypassing capillaries and predisposing young patients to hemorrhagic stroke. Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) can result in curative bAVM obliteration through delayed thrombosis, yet hemorrhage risk persists during the latency period. The mechanisms underlying this delayed response remain unclear. Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), web-like structures of chromatin DNA and granule proteins, have been identified in bAVMs. We investigated whether citrullinated histone H3 (CitH3)-positive cells, used as a surrogate marker of NET-related activity, are associated with post-radiosurgical vascular remodeling in bAVMs.We analyzed the expression of CitH3 in surgical specimens from patients with bAVMs without prior SRS (n = 6), with prior SRS (n = 6), and with epilepsy as controls (n = 2). CitH3 localization in the vessel wall and endoluminal space was examined by immunohistochemistry.CitH3-positive cells were more abundant in both the vessel wall and endoluminal regions of SRS-treated bAVMs compared with untreated bAVMs and controls. In the vessel wall, the mean percentage of CitH3-positive cells was 1.73% in SRS-treated bAVMs, 0.86% in untreated bAVMs, and 0.25% in controls, with a significant increase following SRS compared with control vessels (p = 0.04). In the endoluminal area, the mean percentage was 1.01% in SRS-treated bAVMs, 0.14% in untreated bAVMs, and 0.01% in controls, with SRS-treated bAVMs showing significantly higher levels than both untreated bAVMs (p = 0.02) and controls (p = 0.02).CitH3-positive cells were increased in surgically resected post-SRS bAVMs, with localization in both vessel walls and endoluminal compartments. These findings support a possible association between NET-related pathology and radiosurgery-associated vascular remodeling. Given the small sample size, selected post-SRS surgical cohort, and surrogate nature of CitH3 staining, these results should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating and require validation in further mechanistic and longitudinal studies.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. llm_summary: Brain arteriovenous malformations are abnormal tangles of blood vessels that can cause dangerous bleeding in young people, and doctors use a radiation treatment called stereotactic radiosurgery to seal them off, though the exact way this treatment works remains a mystery. Researchers examined tissue samples from patients who had received this radiation treatment and compared them to samples from patients who had not been treated, looking for signs of neutrophil extracellular traps, which are web-like structures made of DNA and proteins released by immune cells that may play a role in blood vessel changes. The study found that treated patients had significantly more of these trap-related markers in both the vessel walls and the hollow centers of blood vessels compared to untreated patients and control samples. These findings suggest that the immune system's trap-making activity might be connected to how blood vessels change and eventually seal off after radiation treatment, which could help explain why this delayed healing process works. Because this study involved only a small number of patients and looked at tissue samples after surgery rather than following patients over time, the researchers emphasized that these results are preliminary and need to be confirmed with larger, more detailed studies before doctors can fully understand what role these immune structures play.

title: Deceased Donor Kidney Transplantation Versus Continued Dialysis Among Patients Aged 75 Years or Older: A Target Trial Emulation.
abstract: The survival benefit of deceased donor kidney transplantation (DDKT) versus continued dialysis among patients aged ≥75 years remains uncertain due to a lack of randomized trials and limitations of observational study. This study estimated the causal effect of DDKT on survival using a target trial emulation.Target trial emulation with sequential trials framework.Transplant-eligible adults aged ≥75 years who initiated dialysis and were listed in the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network registry (2015-2023) for kidney-only transplantation.DDKT versus remaining on dialysis.Restricted mean survival time (RMST) at 3 and 5 years.The stacked dataset from all auxiliary trials analyzed using weighted Cox proportional hazards regression. Inverse probability of treatment and censoring weights incorporated to address confounding and immortal time bias.Among 2,670 patients (mean age, 76.8 years; 70.7% male; 49% with diabetes), 1,012 (37.9%) received DDKT. The framework generated 511 auxiliary trials with 505,438 person-trial observations. DDKT recipients experienced early mortality risk (HR, 2.29 [95% CI, 1.50-3.49] for days 0-90) transitioning to survival benefit beyond 1 year (HR, 0.34 [95% CI, 0.26-0.45] after 3 years). At 3 years, the break-even point, survival was equivalent between groups (RMST difference, 2.0 days; P = 0.9). By 5 years, DDKT conferred a 111-day survival advantage ([95% CI, 65.6-156.4], P < 0.001). Patients without diabetes experienced a numerically greater benefit than patients with diabetes (133.6 vs 81.2 days; P interaction = 0.3), as did those who received ≥2 years dialysis versus <2 years (156.1 vs 107.9 days; P interaction = 0.3).Unmeasured confounding, generalizability limited to wait-listed patients, most covariates measured at listing rather than updated over time, lack of data on quality of life, symptom burden, or patient-reported outcomes.DDKT confers a survival benefit to wait-listed patients aged ≥75 years although this benefit emerges only after 3 years, providing a critical benchmark for patient counseling. The modest 5-year advantage for DDKT should be weighed against earlier elevated risks of mortality. These findings support individualized decision-making and highlight dialysis as a reasonable alternative to DDKT.Kidney transplantation is the preferred treatment for kidney failure, but whether it benefits patients aged 75 and older remains unclear. Previous studies in this age group have been limited by biased methods. This study used target trial emulation to mimic a randomized trial using national registry data, allowing estimation of transplantation's true effect on patient survival. We found that transplant recipients face a higher mortality risk in the first few months after surgery, but those who survive this early period live longer than patients continuing to receive dialysis. This survival advantage becomes clear after about 3 years of follow-up. These findings can help elderly patients and their nephrologists make more informed decisions and emphasize that age alone should not exclude patients from consideration for kidney transplantation.Copyright © 2026 National Kidney Foundation, Inc.
