llm_summary: Researchers examined the global health workforce across 204 countries from 1990 to 2023 to understand how many doctors, nurses, and other health workers exist and whether there are enough of them to provide good healthcare to everyone. They collected information from surveys, census data, and administrative records, then used statistical methods to estimate the total number of health workers by type and gender across all countries and over time. In 2023, the world had about 122 million health workers, nearly triple the number from 1990, with women making up about 69 percent of the workforce and driving most of the growth in new health worker positions. Despite this growth, major gaps remain, with sub-Saharan Africa having far fewer health workers per person than wealthy countries, and the world still needs millions more doctors, nurses, midwives, dentists, and pharmacists to ensure everyone can access quality healthcare. To close these gaps, countries will need to train more health workers, pay them better, and create work arrangements that support both men and women in healthcare careers.

title: A Generational Approach to Neurology Education: Engaging Generation Z Learners.
abstract: Neurophobia remains a persistent barrier in neurology education because learners often struggle to connect neuroanatomy, localization, examination findings, and clinical reasoning. At the same time, Generation Z learners now comprise much of undergraduate and graduate medical education and have trained in an environment shaped by ubiquitous mobile technology, short-form media, rapid information retrieval, and heightened attention to feedback, well-being, and belonging. This review synthesizes literature on neurophobia, Gen Z learner preferences, cognitive load, active learning, simulation, multimedia instruction, social media, artificial intelligence (AI), and recent Neurology® Education scholarship. It argues for a generationally informed, not generationally deterministic, approach: many recommended strategies predate Gen Z and benefit learners across age groups, but they are especially relevant to the current technologic and cultural learning environment. Practical strategies include selective flipped classrooms, microlearning with spaced retrieval, simulation and deliberate practice, coaching-oriented feedback, curated social media resources, supervised AI use, and psychologically safe teaching cultures. A critical, theory-grounded approach can help neurology educators preserve rigor while making the path into neurologic reasoning clearer.© 2026 American Academy of Neurology.

llm_summary: Neurophobia, which is the fear or discomfort students feel when learning about the nervous system and brain, remains a major problem in medical education because students struggle to connect different pieces of information like anatomy, physical exam findings, and clinical reasoning. The review examined how Generation Z learners, who grew up with smartphones and social media, have different learning preferences than previous generations, including a preference for short lessons, quick feedback, and a sense of belonging in their educational environment. The researchers found that while many effective teaching strategies like flipped classrooms (where students watch videos at home and practice in class), breaking material into small chunks, using simulations, and providing supportive feedback are not new, they are especially valuable for today's learners who are accustomed to technology and rapid information sharing. Neurology educators can make learning clearer and less intimidating by using these practical strategies while maintaining academic rigor, such as carefully using artificial intelligence tools, creating safe learning environments, and sharing curated educational content on social media. The approach emphasizes that teaching methods should be informed by how Generation Z learns best, rather than assuming all young learners are the same, which can help more medical students develop confidence and skill in understanding.

title: Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Therapy of Malignancy in Kidney Transplant Recipients: Analysis of Real-world Outcomes.
abstract: The use of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in kidney transplant recipients (KTR) for cancer treatment is limited by concerns of allograft rejection and uncertain oncologic efficacy.We conducted a single-center retrospective study of KTR with unresectable or metastatic malignancies treated between 2018 and 2025. The primary study cohort included 33 patients treated with ICI, whose outcomes were compared with 20 matched KTR treated with non-ICI systemic chemotherapy (SC).KTR treated with ICI achieved an objective response rate of 36.4% (12/33) versus 30.0% (6/20) with SC, and a clinical benefit rate of 54.5% (18/33) versus 35.0% (7/20); neither difference was statistically significant (objective response rate P = 0.77; clinical benefit rate P = 0.27). Disease progression occurred in 81.8% of ICI-treated patients and 95.0% of SC-treated patients (P = 0.23), and death because of cancer progression occurred in 63.6% and 75.0%, respectively (P = 0.58). Median progression-free survival was 7.3 mo (95% confidence interval [CI], 4.3-10.8 mo) in the ICI group versus 4.1 mo (95% CI, 2.8-6.3 mo) in the SC group (log-rank P = 0.156). Median overall survival was 15.1 mo (95% CI, 7.6-37.3 mo) with ICI versus 8.7 mo (95% CI, 4.9-14.8 mo) with SC (log-rank P = 0.079). Posttreatment allograft rejection occurred in 12.1% of ICI-treated patients and 0.0% of SC-treated patients (P = 0.29), with irreversible graft loss in 3.0%. Grade ≥2 immune-related adverse events occurred in 12.1% of ICI-treated patients, and no treatment-related deaths were observed.ICI therapy was associated with a trend toward longer overall survival when compared with SC and with a low rate of rejection and allograft loss.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Kidney transplant recipients who develop cancer face a difficult choice because the drugs that boost the immune system to fight cancer might also cause the body to reject the transplanted kidney. Researchers studied 33 kidney transplant patients with advanced cancer who received immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy, which works by releasing the brakes on the immune system to attack cancer cells, and compared their outcomes to 20 similar patients who received traditional chemotherapy instead. Patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors showed a trend toward living longer overall, with a median survival of about 15 months compared to about 9 months for those receiving chemotherapy, though the difference was not large enough to be statistically certain. The immune checkpoint inhibitor group did experience kidney rejection in about 12 percent of cases, but only 3 percent lost their transplanted kidney permanently, and serious side effects were uncommon. These findings suggest that immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy may be a reasonable treatment option for kidney transplant recipients with advanced cancer, though doctors should carefully monitor patients for signs of transplant rejection.

title: Impact of vasomotor symptoms on women in the workplace: Results from a non-interventional survey in the United States.
abstract: Vasomotor symptoms are experienced by up to 80% of postmenopausal women. Women were surveyed to evaluate the impact of vasomotor symptoms in the workplace, support from employers/colleagues, and perceptions of workplace accommodations.Participants aged 40-65 years were recruited from Dynata panels for an electronic survey. Women were experiencing vasomotor symptoms for ≥1 month with ≥2 hot flash/night sweat episodes per day in the preceding 2 weeks and were currently employed or had stopped working/retired within the last year.Demographic characteristics and Work Productivity and Activity Impairment.Respondents (N = 1011) were mostly White (72.9%), with a mean (standard deviation) age 49.6 (6.4) years, reporting a mean of 7.5 (11.1) hot flashes or night sweats per day in the preceding 2 weeks. The majority (81.3%) had never received treatment. Activity impairment, absenteeism, and presenteeism were reported by 36%, 6%, and 32%, respectively, and increased with increasing vasomotor symptom severity. Almost 80% of respondents had not discussed vasomotor symptoms with their employer; only 18.1% indicated employer support for vasomotor symptoms. Top coping mechanisms at work were temperature control (71.0%) and wearing layered, breathable clothing (46.0%). Respondents suggested some work accommodations for vasomotor symptoms: changes to benefit packages (27.9%), creating more workplace awareness (25.7%), and more flexible working arrangements (23.2%).Despite demonstrable adverse effects of vasomotor symptoms on United States women in the workplace, treatment rates were very low. Enhanced awareness regarding treatment options alongside potential workplace accommodations may improve work productivity, employee satisfaction, and retention.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. llm_summary: Vasomotor symptoms, which are hot flashes and night sweats that affect up to 80 percent of women going through menopause, can significantly interfere with their ability to work and be productive. Researchers surveyed over 1,000 women aged 40 to 65 who were currently employed or had recently stopped working and were experiencing at least two hot flashes or night sweats per day to understand how these symptoms affected their jobs and what support they received from employers. The study found that more than one-third of women reported difficulty completing their work activities, nearly one-third struggled with presenteeism (being at work but not fully productive), and about 6 percent missed work entirely, with these problems getting worse as symptoms became more severe. Despite these serious workplace challenges, 81 percent of the women had never received any medical treatment for their symptoms, and almost 80 percent had never even discussed the issue with their employer. The researchers concluded that increasing awareness about available treatments and offering workplace accommodations like flexible schedules and temperature control could help women stay productive at work and remain in their jobs.

title: Phenobarbital Versus Benzodiazepine-Based Pathways for Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome in Critically Ill Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: To compare outcomes of phenobarbital-based versus benzodiazepine-based pathways for alcohol withdrawal syndrome (AWS) in critically ill adults and evaluate whether pathway design and timing of phenobarbital use affect treatment outcomes.A librarian-led search of MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central, CINAHL, Web of Science, Scopus, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform was conducted through July 2024, with updates in December 2024, August 2025, and December 2025. Search concepts included phenobarbital, benzodiazepines, and alcohol withdrawal.Comparative studies of adults admitted or transferred to an intensive care unit (ICU) with AWS and treated with phenobarbital-based versus benzodiazepine-based pathways were included. Sixteen nonrandomized studies were included in the qualitative synthesis, and 12 treatment-oriented studies were included in the primary meta-analysis. Multiple reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies-of Interventions (ROBINS-I).Phenobarbital-based pathways were not associated with significantly different intubation (11 studies; odds ratio (OR), 0.62; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.20-1.87; I2 = 73%) or hospital length of stay (five studies; mean differences [MD], -1.75 days; 95% CI, -5.07 to 1.56; I2 = 63%) compared with benzodiazepine-based pathways. ICU length of stay was shorter with phenobarbital-based pathways (eight studies; MD, -0.60 days; 95% CI, -0.79 to -0.41; I2 = 0%). In exploratory subgroup analyses, front-loaded, protocolized phenobarbital-first pathways were associated with lower intubation and shorter hospital length of stay, but certainty of evidence was very low.This review distinguishes phenobarbital-first, protocolized ICU pathways from adjunctive or mixed phenobarbital strategies, suggesting that implementation design may influence outcomes.Although evidence remains very low certainty, these findings suggest that phenobarbital's role in ICU AWS may be pathway dependent. llm_summary: Researchers examined how two different treatment approaches work for alcohol withdrawal syndrome, a serious medical condition that occurs when people stop drinking alcohol, in patients admitted to intensive care units. The team reviewed sixteen previous studies comparing phenobarbital, a type of sedative medication, against benzodiazepines, another class of sedative drugs commonly used for this condition, by searching medical databases through 2025. The results showed that phenobarbital-based treatment did not significantly reduce the need for breathing tubes or how long patients stayed in the hospital overall, but patients treated with phenobarbital did spend slightly less time in the intensive care unit. When researchers looked more closely at studies using a specific approach called front-loaded, protocolized phenobarbital-first pathways, meaning giving phenobarbital as the main treatment from the start according to a set plan, these patients appeared to have better outcomes with lower rates of needing breathing tubes and shorter hospital stays. Although these findings are promising, the researchers emphasized that the evidence is not yet strong enough to make definitive recommendations and that larger, well-designed studies are needed to confirm whether this specific treatment approach truly works better than current standard care.

title: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes and breast radiotherapy: perspectives from the International Immuno-Oncology Biomarker Working Group.
abstract: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) are prognostic and predictive biomarkers in breast cancer. High pre-treatment TILs are associated with a favourable prognosis and improved response to systemic therapies. However, the role of TILs in mediating response to radiotherapy in breast cancer remains underexplored, with scarce clinical evidence to date. In this Review, we present an overview of current evidence and potential mechanisms, highlight opportunities for integrating TILs into radiation oncology trials and clinical practice, and call for standardised TIL reporting to accelerate biomarker-driven individualisation of radiotherapy in breast cancer.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. llm_summary: Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, which are immune cells found within cancer tissue, are important markers that can predict how well breast cancer patients will respond to treatment and what their long-term outlook might be. Researchers from an international working group reviewed existing evidence about how these immune cells affect breast cancer patients who receive radiation therapy, a common cancer treatment that uses high-energy beams to destroy cancer cells. The review found that while high levels of these immune cells before treatment are linked to better outcomes and improved response to drug therapies, their role in helping patients respond to radiation therapy has not been thoroughly studied or understood. The authors are calling for doctors and researchers to start measuring and reporting these immune cell levels in a consistent way across all breast cancer radiation therapy trials so that treatment can be personalized based on each patient's individual immune profile. Moving forward, integrating immune cell measurements into radiation therapy planning and clinical practice could help doctors better predict which patients will benefit most from radiation and potentially improve how breast cancer is treated.

title: Proteomic alterations in patient bone-derived stromal cells and their secretomes in osteogenesis imperfecta.
abstract: Type I collagen is the most abundant form of collagen and forms the organic component of bone. Pathogenic variants in genes encoding its constituent polypeptide chains, COL1A1 and COL1A2, can result in autosomal dominant osteogenesis imperfecta and other connective tissue disorders. Although osteogenesis imperfecta is clinically well-described, the molecular basis of clinical heterogeneity among patients is not well understood. We undertook a global proteomic approach to uncover alterations in osteogenesis imperfecta patient bone-derived stromal cells as well as their secretome. We performed multiplexed tandem mass tag (TMT)-based proteomics analysis of cells from three patients along with three controls to investigate global changes in the proteome of these cells as well as their secretome. This was combined with analysis of proline hydroxylation to catalog the modification of type I collagens in this disorder. We observed significant changes in both the cellular and secreted proteomes including the levels of proteins involved in osteoblast proliferation such as nitric oxide synthase-interacting protein (NOSIP), secreted frizzled-related protein 1 (SRFP1) and transforming growth factor beta-1-induced transcript 1 protein (TGFB1I1) as well as others involved in endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis such as protein disulfide isomerase A6 (PDIA6) and reticulophagy regulator 3 (RETREG3). Notably, a number of alterations were observed in proline hydroxylation in intracellular collagens - COL1A1 and COL1A2. These findings expand our current understanding of the cellular pathophysiology in osteogenesis imperfecta and could lead to the identification of novel therapeutic targets.© 2026 Published by Elsevier Inc.

llm_summary: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a genetic bone disease caused by problems in genes that make collagen, which is the main protein that gives bones their strength and structure. Researchers used advanced laboratory techniques to examine bone cells from three patients with this disease and three healthy people, looking at all the proteins present in both the cells themselves and the substances the cells released into their surroundings. The scientists discovered that patients with osteogenesis imperfecta had significant changes in many proteins, including some that help bone cells grow and divide, as well as proteins that manage stress inside cells when they are making collagen. They also found that the collagen proteins in patient cells had unusual chemical modifications, particularly in a component called proline, which suggested the cells were struggling to properly process and assemble collagen. These findings provide new insights into how osteogenesis imperfecta damages bone cells at the molecular level and could help scientists develop new treatments to help patients with this serious genetic disorder.

title: SOHO State-of-the-Art Updates and Next Questions: Current Approach to Waldenström Macroglobulinemia.
abstract: Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM) or Immunoglobulin M (IgM) lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma is a heterogeneous clinicopathologic entity with distinguishing features that include circulating monoclonal IgM, lymphoplasmacytic marrow infiltrate, and in > 90% of patients, a recurrent clonal mutation, MYD88L265. The clinical manifestations are highly variable. Symptomatic patients with indication(s) to start therapy are initially managed with either fixed-duration chemoimmunotherapy (for example, bendamustine-rituximab) or a covalent Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor (for example, zanubrutinib) given until progression or intolerable toxicity, although these 2 highly different approaches have not been directly compared in randomized trials. MYD88L265P, CXCR4, and TP53 mutational status may potentially impact treatment decision-making. Options for managing WM are expanding as several recent trials demonstrate the promising efficacy of BCL-2 inhibitors, noncovalent BTK inhibitors and BTK degraders in patients that are previously exposed, or refractory, to a covalent BTK inhibitor and/or chemoimmunotherapy. Preliminary data with novel approaches involving CAR-T cell and bispecific antibodies are continuing to be generated, and the reports, thus far, are encouraging.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a rare blood cancer where the body produces abnormal proteins called immunoglobulin M, and more than nine out of ten patients have a specific genetic mutation that doctors can test for. Doctors currently treat patients who have symptoms with either chemotherapy combined with an immune-boosting drug or with a targeted therapy called a Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor, which blocks a protein that helps cancer cells grow. Recent research shows that newer treatment options like drugs that target a protein called BCL-2, different types of kinase inhibitors, and even experimental cell-based therapies called CAR-T cells are showing promising results, especially for patients whose cancer has stopped responding to the standard treatments. The genetic mutations present in each patient's cancer cells may help doctors choose which treatment will work best, though more research is needed to understand how to use this information most effectively. As treatment options continue to expand and improve, doctors will need to conduct more direct comparisons between different approaches to determine which patients benefit most from each therapy.

title: Designing Integrated Virtual Care Partnerships: Insights from a Practice-Based Case Series at Mayo Clinic.
abstract: Access to high-quality primary and specialty care remains a persistent challenge in the United States, with millions of individuals facing barriers due to geography, provider shortages, and health inequities. As health care systems seek innovative solutions, virtual care providers have emerged as critical partners in expanding access, enhancing continuity, and supporting transitions across the health care continuum. This manuscript explores the integration of virtual care providers within an academic medical center, highlighting the dual roles of collaborative and referral models in bridging gaps between traditional outpatient care and virtual health services. Drawing on practical experience, we identify core design principles (acute access, continuity, convenience, cost, reach, and transitions) that underpin successful partnerships and sustainable adoption. These insights underscore the importance of aligning virtual care provider relationships with existing organizational culture, secure data sharing, and supportive reimbursement structures. As academic medical centers and health systems nationwide navigate the evolving landscape of virtual health, thoughtful integration of virtual care providers offers a pathway to address disparities, improve patient outcomes, and advance the quality and reach of care delivery.© 2026 The Authors.

llm_summary: Millions of Americans struggle to access quality medical care due to living far from hospitals, not having enough doctors in their area, and facing other unfair barriers to healthcare. Researchers at Mayo Clinic, a major academic medical center, studied how to better integrate virtual care providers, which are doctors and nurses who deliver care through video and phone calls, into their existing healthcare system. They found that successful partnerships between traditional in-person clinics and virtual care services work best when they focus on six key principles: quick access to urgent care, continuous relationships with patients, convenience for patients, affordable costs, the ability to reach more people, and smooth transitions between different types of care. The study shows that for these partnerships to work well and last, healthcare systems need to support them with good data sharing between computer systems, payment structures that reward virtual care, and a workplace culture that values this new approach. These findings suggest that thoughtfully combining virtual care providers with traditional hospitals and clinics could help reduce healthcare inequalities, improve how well patients do, and make quality medical care available to more people across the country.

title: Wearable-derived measures of stress physiology in patients with opioid use disorder treated with methadone: A stress-task study in a real-world clinic with healthy controls.
abstract: Wearable biosensors enable real-time monitoring of physiological stress. While methadone maintenance treatment (MMT) is effective in opioid use disorder (OUD), inter-dose withdrawal and stress dysregulation remain challenges. We sought to identify wearable-derived digital biomarkers of stress in individuals with OUD receiving MMT.In this cross-sectional, laboratory-based study, 72 adults completed 76 sessions (14 OUD pre-methadone dose, 15 OUD post-dose, 47 healthy controls) of a standardized protocol of calm tasks (e.g., relaxing videos, positive memory recall) followed by stress-inducing tasks (e.g., horror video, mental arithmetic, negative memory recall). Physiological data were continuously recorded using the Empatica E4 wristband (heart rate, heart rate variability [HRV], electrodermal activity [EDA], skin temperature, accelerometry). Features were extracted using open-source toolkits. Linear mixed-effects models tested calm-stress differences and group effects; Random Forest classifiers evaluated calm versus stress classification.Among 340 extracted features, 63 (18.5%) significantly differentiated calm from stress across all groups, with EDA- and accelerometry-derived features showing the most consistent stress sensitivity. Compared with controls, OUD participants demonstrated higher baseline arousal and altered stress reactivity, with the largest responses observed in the pre-dose group. Random Forest models performed best for cognitively demanding tasks (up to 98% accuracy) and more modestly for other tasks.Wearable sensors can detect multidimensional alterations in resting-state physiology and stress reactivity among individuals with OUD on methadone. Future studies should validate these candidate biomarkers and test whether integrating wearable-derived stress detection into treatment improves clinically meaningful outcomes, such as stress management, craving, risk of return to opioid use, and retention.© 2026 The Authors.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether wearable devices like smartwatches could detect stress responses in people with opioid use disorder who were receiving methadone treatment, a medication that helps reduce opioid cravings and withdrawal symptoms. The study involved 72 adults who wore a special wristband that measured heart rate, skin electrical activity, and other body signals while they completed calm activities like watching relaxing videos and then stressful tasks like watching scary movies or doing difficult math problems. The results showed that people with opioid use disorder had higher baseline stress levels and different stress responses compared to healthy people without opioid problems, with the biggest differences appearing in those measured before they received their daily methadone dose. These findings suggest that wearable sensors could potentially help doctors monitor stress in real time and identify when patients are at higher risk of returning to opioid use or struggling with cravings. Future research needs to test whether using this wearable technology to track and manage stress actually helps patients stay in treatment and avoid relapsing to opioid use.

title: Clinical benefit of optimization of heart failure therapy after heart failure hospitalization in adults with CHD.
abstract: Heart failure (HF) hospitalization is a marker of HF progression, and it is associated with mortality in adults with congenital heart disease (CHD). The purpose of this study was to assess the effect of guideline directed medical therapy (GDMT) on HF readmission and mortality in CHD patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). We hypothesized that higher GDMT use was associated with lower risk of HF readmission and mortality.Retrospective study of CHD patients and HFrEF, admitted for HF (2003-2023). GDMT use was assessed at hospital discharge (baseline) and 1-year follow-up using a standardized GDMT score. GDMT uptitration was assessed as difference between GDMT score at baseline versus 1-year follow-up.Of 153 patients (age 51 ± 15 years, 39% males, left ventricular EF 29 ± 7%), the median baseline GDMT score was 2 (1, 3). Baseline GDMT score was associated with lower risk of HF readmission (hazard ratio [HR] 0.73, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.54, 0.92, p < 0.001) and mortality (HR 0.71, 95%CI 0.50, 0.93, p < 0.001) per 1-unit increase in baseline GDMT score. Among patients with 1-year follow-up (N = 128), GDMT uptitration was associated with lower risk of HF readmission (HR 0.72, 95%CI 0.49, 0.94, p < 0.001) and mortality (HR 0.69, 95%CI 0.41, 0.92, p = 0.02) per 1-unit increase. Patients with GDMT uptitration (N = 49, 38%) had greater improvement in neurohormonal activation and left ventricular systolic function, consistent with a lower risk of HF readmission and mortality in that group.GDMT optimization was associated with lower risk of HF readmission and all-cause mortality amongst adults with CHD. Further studies are required to determine whether strategies to improve GDMT optimization would improve clinical outcomes in this population.© 2026 The Authors.

llm_summary: Heart failure, a condition where the heart cannot pump blood effectively, is a serious problem for adults born with heart defects, and hospitalization for this condition often leads to worse outcomes and death. Researchers looked back at medical records from 2003 to 2023 for 153 patients with heart defects and reduced heart pumping ability who were hospitalized for heart failure, tracking how well doctors followed treatment guidelines and measuring whether patients were readmitted to the hospital or died. Patients who were prescribed more of the recommended heart failure medications at hospital discharge had a lower chance of being readmitted to the hospital and a lower risk of death, and this benefit was even greater for patients whose medication doses were increased over the following year. The study shows that when doctors optimize, or carefully adjust, heart failure medications according to medical guidelines in patients with heart defects, these patients experience better heart function and have fewer hospital readmissions and lower death rates. The researchers conclude that improving how well doctors follow medication guidelines could help patients with heart defects and heart failure live longer and healthier lives, though more research is needed to test whether specific strategies to increase medication use would actually improve patient outcomes.

title: Phenotype tailored lifestyle intervention for weight management in individuals with emotional eating: A secondary analysis of the PHENO-Diet trial.
abstract: In a proof-of-concept trial, a phenotype tailored lifestyle intervention (PLI) led to greater weight loss than a standardized lifestyle intervention (SLI). This secondary analysis evaluated the effect of the PLI for individuals with an emotional eating phenotype (EE) on weight loss outcomes, eating behaviors and mood.This original clinical research article is a secondary analysis of a 12-week, non-randomized, date-of-treatment trial in which adults with obesity underwent phenotyping and were assigned sequentially to either a PLI (N = 84) or a SLI (N = 81). The EE phenotype was defined as a HADS-A (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale for Anxiety) score ≥7. Weight loss outcome and changes in eating behaviors and mood were evaluated among participants with EE assigned to an SLI (n = 19) or a PLI (n = 26).Participants with EE assigned to the PLI achieved greater weight loss at 12-weeks compared with those assigned to the SLI (-5.9% ± 4.4 vs. -2.6% ± 4.8; p = 0.02). Participants with EE assigned to the PLI demonstrated reduced HADS-A and HADS-D scores, and the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire Emotional Eating subscale (TFEQ-EE), while those assigned to the SLI had minimal or no improvements after 12-weeks. Among participants with EE assigned to the PLI, Higher HADS-A scores and lower scores in the Weight Efficacy Lifestyle questionnaire (WEL) negative emotions subscale and TFEQ-EE at baseline were associated with greater weight loss at 12-weeks. (NCT04073394).These findings support tailoring behavioral weight-loss interventions for adults with obesity and EE. Larger randomized studies with longer follow-up are needed to further refine phenotype-based approaches.© 2026 The Authors.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a personalized weight loss program could work better than a standard program for people with obesity who tend to eat more when they feel anxious or sad. In this 12-week study, adults with obesity were assigned to either a tailored program designed specifically for their eating patterns or a standard program, with special focus on those showing signs of emotional eating through anxiety screening. People who received the personalized program lost significantly more weight, about 5. 9 percent of their body weight compared to 2. 6 percent in the standard program group, and they also showed improvements in anxiety, depression, and emotional eating behaviors.

title: Moving beyond anatomy: the future of rectal cancer management is biologically-informed, response-adapted, and patient-centered.
abstract: The purpose of this correspondence is to expand upon the recent review article by Noiret et al. addressing management of locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) and proposing anatomically guided treatment strategies. While tumor location influences surgical complexity and functional outcomes, we caution against an overly anatomy centric framework that may oversimplify treatment selection and underemphasize patient preferences and biological determinants of response. Current evidence does not support the assertion that chemotherapy followed by surgery provides superior long-term functional outcomes compared with total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) with organ preservation (OP). Contemporary management of LARC includes multiple curative-intent strategies, each associated with distinct tradeoffs in oncologic control, toxicity, and quality of life. In particular, modern radiotherapy techniques and OP strategies have demonstrated favorable response rates, functional outcomes, and quality of life compared with radical surgery. We argue that future treatment paradigms should move beyond anatomy alone and prioritize biologic risk stratification, response adaptive treatment, and incorporation of multi-omic biomarkers. Ultimately, treatment decisions should integrate patient preferences, oncologic risk, functional outcomes, and evolving biologic understanding to optimize individualized care for patients with LARC.© 2026 The Author(s).

llm_summary: Treatment decisions for locally advanced rectal cancer, which is cancer that has grown into surrounding tissues or nearby lymph nodes, have traditionally focused too much on where the tumor is located in the body rather than on the individual patient's needs and the cancer's biological characteristics. Researchers and doctors argue that current evidence does not support the idea that chemotherapy followed by surgery is better for long-term quality of life than total neoadjuvant therapy, which is giving strong cancer-fighting drugs and radiation before surgery to shrink the tumor. Modern radiation techniques and strategies that preserve the organ, meaning avoiding complete surgical removal of the rectum when possible, have shown good results with favorable survival rates, fewer side effects, and better quality of life compared with traditional surgery that removes the entire rectum. The authors recommend that future treatment plans should combine biological risk assessment, meaning testing the cancer to understand how aggressive it is, with personalized treatment approaches that adapt based on how well the cancer responds to initial therapy. Treatment decisions should ultimately be tailored to each patient by weighing their personal preferences, the cancer's risk level, expected side effects, and what scientists learn about the cancer's biology to provide the best possible care.

title: National study of medical education, ethical attitudes and curricular exposure to voluntary assisted dying by VOICE (Views Of Incoming Clinicians on End-of-life care).
abstract: Legislative moves to legalise assisted dying in the UK have renewed discussion on future clinicians' preparedness for new potential responsibilities. This study examined medical students' ethical attitudes, legal understanding and curricular exposure.VOICE was a national cross-sectional survey of UK and Ireland medical students in 2025 (n = 896). The questionnaire assessed ethical views, confidence, legal knowledge and teaching exposure. Descriptive statistics, thematic analysis and multivariable logistic regression explored predictors of ethical agreement, curriculum coverage and legal knowledge.Most students (64.5%) believed that assisted dying can be ethically justified, yet legal knowledge was limited; only 7.6% correctly identified all eligibility criteria. Nearly 70% reported minimal curricular coverage. Formal teaching was associated with higher confidence and greater ethical agreement. Regional variation and concerns about coercion and inequalities were common.Students show broad ethical support but have very limited confidence, legal understanding and curricular preparation, highlighting the need for structured education.© 2026 The Authors.

Researchers surveyed nearly 900 medical students from the UK and Ireland in 2025 to understand their personal beliefs about assisted dying, how much they knew about the legal rules, and what they had learned about it in school. The study found that most students, about two-thirds, thought assisted dying could be morally acceptable, but very few of them actually understood the legal requirements, with only 7. 6 percent knowing all the eligibility rules correctly. Nearly 70 percent of students reported that their medical schools taught them very little about this topic, though those who did receive formal teaching felt more confident and were more likely to support assisted dying.

title: Multicentric Calcifying Aponeurotic Fibroma of the Upper Extremity With Associated Nerve Compression and Bony Dysplasia.
abstract: A 19-year-old woman with presumed history of lymphatic malformation of her right elbow and wrist with intermittent mild pain, positive Tinel sign at the proximal forearm, elbow contracture, and limited pronosupination presented for a second opinion. She had been diagnosed clinically with a vascular malformation in infancy with subsequent magnetic resonance imaging findings of a fatty tumor versus malformation. She was treated conservatively with splinting for her range of motion limitations for years. Ultimately, magnetic resonance-guided biopsy demonstrated calcifying aponeurotic fibroma (CAF). Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging further demonstrated a dysplastic distal radioulnar joint and fatty muscle atrophy at the proximal forearm. Excisional biopsy of the two lesions demonstrated multicentric CAF. Multicentric CAF is exceedingly rare as are associated nerve compression and bony dysplasia. This case adds to our collective knowledge on CAF to better elucidate the pathogenesis as well as bring greater awareness of this rare tumor to aid practitioners in avoiding misdiagnoses as in our patient.© 2026 The Authors.

Doctors used imaging tests including magnetic resonance imaging, which takes detailed pictures of the body's soft tissues, and a biopsy, which is a small tissue sample examined under a microscope, to finally identify the correct diagnosis after years of unsuccessful conservative treatment with splinting. The imaging revealed that this patient had an unusually rare form of the disease called multicentric calcifying aponeurotic fibroma, meaning multiple tumors of this type were present in different locations, along with nerve compression and abnormal bone development in her wrist joint. This case is particularly important because multicentric calcifying aponeurotic fibroma is extremely uncommon, and the combination with nerve compression and bone problems makes it even more unusual and valuable for medical knowledge. Doctors hope that sharing this case will help other healthcare providers recognize this rare tumor more quickly and avoid the years of misdiagnosis and ineffective.

title: Arthroscopically and manually minced cartilage demonstrates lower cell viability and lower proteoglycan deposition compared to isolated chondrons and chondrocytes.
abstract: Autologous minced cartilage offers a single-stage, low-cost alternative to cell therapies for treatment of chondral defects. It is often derived from debrided defects or loose bodies, then minced for reimplantation. However, there is a paucity of knowledge on how mincing cartilage impacts viability and extracellular matrix deposition compared to quality-controlled cell therapies. The purpose is therefore to better characterize minced cartilage by comparing different mincing techniques to isolated cells.Cartilage samples were obtained from fresh human osteochondral allografts (JRF Ortho) and divided into: chondral allograft biopsy (control), manually minced cartilage, arthroscopically minced cartilage, isolated chondrons, and isolated chondrocytes. Samples were embedded in fibrin gels and cultured for 28 days. Staining for viability and histology for collagen and proteoglycan components were performed. Cartilage samples derived from debrided defects or loose bodies were evaluated for sulphated glycosaminoglycans (sGAGs), DNA, and wet weight.At 28 days, viability of chondrons (93.7 ± 2.9%), chondrocytes (94 ± 22%) and manually minced cartilage (79.8 ± 16.2%) were significantly higher than arthroscopically minced cartilage (56.6 ± 15.4%). Over time, isolated cells showed proteoglycan and type II collagen deposition, while minced cartilage groups showed reduced proteoglycan content on histology. Clinical cartilage samples varied >10-fold in wet weight, total DNA, sGAGs/weight, and DNA/weight.This study showed isolated cells have consistently high viability and deposit more proteoglycans over time compared to both minced cartilage groups. Samples typically used for clinical application of minced cartilage can vary over 10-fold in cellularity and proteoglycan content. As consequences for treatment effect are unknown, implementation in clinical practice without quality regulation is not recommended.© 2026 The Authors.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether minced cartilage, a simple and affordable treatment option for damaged joints, works as well as more advanced cell-based therapies that require extra processing steps. The team compared different ways of breaking up cartilage tissue with isolated cells by growing them in gel for four weeks and measuring how many cells survived and how much new cartilage material they produced. They found that isolated cells and manually minced cartilage had much higher survival rates than cartilage minced with arthroscopic tools, and isolated cells produced significantly more protective cartilage components called proteoglycans over time. The clinical samples of minced cartilage that doctors typically use varied dramatically in quality, with some samples containing ten times more cells and cartilage material than others, which could affect how well the treatment works for patients. The researchers concluded that using minced cartilage without quality control standards is risky because the treatment's effectiveness cannot be guaranteed, and they recommend that future clinical use should include standardized quality checks.

title: The damaged connectome: Mechanisms and consequences of brain network reorganization following neurotrauma.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) represents a major cause of chronic disability worldwide, with outcomes that are notoriously heterogeneous and difficult to predict. This heterogeneity stems from the fact that TBI is not merely a focal injury but a whole-brain network disorder. The brain's structural and functional organization-the connectome-is profoundly disrupted by traumatic forces. However, the post-injury period is not static; it is characterized by a dynamic, multi-stage process of reorganization that unfolds from hours to years. This review synthesizes current evidence on how neurotrauma dismantles brain networks and how the brain subsequently attempts to repair and reconfigure itself. We explore the cellular and systems-level mechanisms of neuroplasticity, the advanced neuroimaging techniques used to measure network changes, and the critical distinction between adaptive and maladaptive reorganization. Finally, we discuss the therapeutic implications of this network-oriented perspective, highlighting neuromodulation, cognitive rehabilitation, and pharmacological interventions as tools to guide recovery, and conclude by outlining key future directions for the field.© 2026 Published by Elsevier Inc.

llm_summary: Traumatic brain injury, which occurs when the head experiences a severe blow or impact, is a leading cause of long-term disability around the world, yet doctors struggle to predict how individual patients will recover because each injury affects the brain differently. This review examines how traumatic brain injury damages the brain's network of connections, which scientists call the connectome, and how the brain attempts to heal and reorganize itself over time through a complex process that can take months or even years. Researchers looked at both the cellular level changes and larger brain system changes that occur during recovery, as well as the advanced imaging techniques that allow doctors to see these network changes happening in the brain. The authors emphasize that some types of brain reorganization after injury help patients recover better, while other types can actually make outcomes worse, and they discuss treatments like brain stimulation therapy, cognitive training, and medications that might guide the brain toward healing. Future research needs to better understand which reorganization patterns lead to good recovery versus poor outcomes so that doctors can develop more targeted treatments to help traumatic brain injury patients regain lost abilities.

title: Distilling Knowledge in Gastroenterology: An Artificial Intelligence System for Assisting Colonoscopy and Pathology Report Review.
abstract: To develop an efficient and domain-adapted system to process colonoscopy and pathology reports using knowledge distillation techniques.We implemented a knowledge distillation framework to create a smaller, domain-specific large language models-based natural language processing model for summarizing and extracting key information from clinical reports. The model was trained on a dataset consisting of 5500 colonoscopy reports and 7000 pathology reports taken from January 1, 2024, to June 30, 2024. Performance was evaluated against ground truth polyp categories derived from pathology report diagnoses.The distilled model reported high domain-specific performance, achieving 95.2% accuracy (95% CI, 93.9%-96.5%), 0.95 precision, and a 31.5% improvement in inference speed relative to the teacher model. Despite being substantially smaller than the teacher model, it maintained strong capability in polyp category identification from key clinical factors, including polyp number, size, histology, and location across colonoscopy and pathology reports. Domain clinicians reported high agreement with model outputs across all 6 evaluated clinical questions, confirming its reliability for supporting follow-up recommendation workflows.This work presents a step toward making domain-specific natural language processing models for gastroenterology more efficient and scalable. By leveraging knowledge distillation, we report the potential for creating more practical domain-specific models that can assist in interpreting complex clinical documentation. Future work will focus on real-world validation and expanding the model to other procedural report types.

title: Silibinin is a natural molecular glue that inhibits PD-L1 glycomaturation.
abstract: The adaptive upregulation of the immune-checkpoint PD-L1 in response to interferon-γ (IFNγ) protects solid tumors from cytotoxic lymphocytes and undermines adoptive cell immunotherapies. Currently, pharmacologically interrupting the trafficking of nascent PD-L1 to the surface of cancer cells is not feasible in a clinical setting.We investigated whether silibinin (SBN), the primary bioactive flavonolignan found in Silybum marianum (milk thistle) seeds, could impede the post-translational glycomaturation of PD-L1 and enhance T-cell-mediated antitumor cytotoxicity.We assessed the effects of SBN on PD-L1 glycomaturation by integrating electrophoretic mobility shifts, Endo-H/PNGase-F glycosidase sensitivity mapping, transcript-level glyco-enzyme arrays, computational molecular dynamics (MD), biochemical cross-linking, AlphaLISA binding, and flow cytometry. Co-cultures of cancer cells with cytokine-activated T cells were performed using SBN as a single agent or in combination with the small-molecule PD-L1 inhibitor BMS-1166.SBN converted nascent PD-L1 into an Endo H-sensitive, 43 kDa, high-mannose species that becomes trapped in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), regardless of STAT3 status. SBN did not alter CD274/PD-L1 transcription or global N-glycosylation. MD predicted, and BS3 cross-linking confirmed, weak but significant SBN-induced PD-L1 dimerization which diminished PD-1 binding. SBN increased the ability of BMS-1166, which also induces PD-L1 dimerization and ER retention of underglycosylated PD-L1, to block PD-1/PD-L1 interaction and to eradicate IFNγ-elicited plasma-membrane PD-L1. SBN was synthetically lethal with BMS-1166, causing multiple cancer types to become highly responsive to the immunocytolytic activity of T cells.SBN is a plant-derived molecular glue that intercepts PD-L1 glycomaturation co-translationally in the ER. When combined with canonical PD-L1 dimerizers, SBN collapses adaptive PD-L1 expression and renders cancer cells exquisitely susceptible to the cytolytic insults of T cells. Due to its favorable safety profile and oral bioavailability, SBN is a promising "glycotherapeutic" phytochemical for T-cell-based immunotherapy, particularly in IFN-rich tumors with reactive PD-L1 expression programs.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Researchers examined whether silibinin, a natural compound found in milk thistle seeds, could prevent cancer cells from hiding from the immune system by blocking a protein called PD-L1 that helps tumors escape detection. The team used multiple laboratory techniques including computer modeling, chemical tests, and cell cultures to study how silibinin affects PD-L1 and whether it could work alongside existing cancer drugs. They found that silibinin traps newly formed PD-L1 proteins inside cancer cells before they can reach the cell surface, and when combined with another drug called BMS-1166, it dramatically reduced the amount of PD-L1 available to shield tumors from immune attack. The combination treatment made cancer cells much more vulnerable to being killed by immune cells called T cells, which are the body's natural defense against cancer. Because silibinin is a plant-based compound that is safe to take by mouth, it could potentially become a new type of treatment to help T-cell immunotherapy work better against certain cancers, though more testing in patients would be needed to confirm these laboratory findings.

llm_summary: Background:  Telomere biology disorders are rare genetic conditions where the protective caps on the ends of chromosomes, called telomeres, become abnormally short or don't function properly, leading to problems with cell division and increased health risks. People with these disorders have been known to develop certain cancers at higher rates than the general population, but this study examines a large group of adult patients to better understand the full range of cancer types that may be associated with these conditions.

title: Early Treatment Failure in Patients Receiving Ciltacabtagene-Autoleucel for Relapsed/Refractory Multiple Myeloma.
abstract: Ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel) has demonstrated excellent efficacy and long-term disease control in patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM). However, a proportion of patients experience early treatment failures. We investigated clinical factors associated with early progression or death (within 12 months) in patients with RRMM receiving standard-of-care cilta-cel across the three Mayo clinic centers. Patients with a follow-up of at least 12 months or progression or death within 12 months from infusion were included. Of the patients with early treatment failure (n = 52), 69% had progressive disease and 31% had a non-relapse mortality (NRM) event. In patients without early treatment failure (n = 164), 13% of events were NRM. Among pretreatment factors, prior BCMA-directed therapy, presence of extramedullary disease and a CAR-HEMATOTOX score of ≥ 2 were independent predictors of early progression or death. The utilization of cilta-cel in earlier lines of treatment (1-3 vs. 4 or more) demonstrated comparable PFS (12-month PFS 73% vs. 77%, p = 0.94). Measurable residual disease positivity in the bone marrow at 3 months (11/197 patients) identified a small but high-risk group with an increased risk of early treatment failure (OR 5.68; p = 0.012). Patients with less than a complete response on a FDG PET/CT at 3 months also had an increased risk of early treatment failure (OR 11.8; p < 0.0001). Our findings may help identify patients at high-risk for early adverse outcomes despite receiving highly effective therapy, and support consideration of novel therapeutic strategies within a clinical trial setting.© 2026 Wiley Periodicals LLC.

llm_summary: Researchers examined a cancer treatment called ciltacabtagene autoleucel, which is a type of therapy where doctors take a patient's own immune cells, modify them in a lab to fight multiple myeloma cancer, and put them back into the body. The study looked at 216 patients with advanced multiple myeloma who received this treatment at three Mayo Clinic centers to find out which patients experienced early treatment failure, meaning their cancer came back or they died within 12 months of receiving the therapy. Among the patients who had early treatment failure, about 69 percent had cancer that continued to grow and 31 percent died from causes other than cancer progression, while patients without early failure had much lower death rates from non-cancer causes. The researchers found that patients who had previously received other treatments targeting a protein called BCMA, those with cancer that had spread outside the bone marrow, and those with a high toxicity score before treatment were at greatest risk for early failure, and patients who still had detectable cancer cells three months after treatment or who did not achieve a complete response on imaging scans were also at high risk. These findings could help doctors identify which patients might benefit from additional or different.

title: Clinical Trial: Effectiveness and Safety of a Novel Anal Insert Device for Treatment of Faecal Incontinence.
abstract: Treatment options for medically-refractory faecal incontinence (FI)-including anorectal biofeedback, dextranomer injection, and sacral nerve stimulation-are limited and outcomes are often suboptimal. Anal or vaginal insert devices are infrequently used.We evaluated the safety and effectiveness of a new anal insert device (StaySure) in patients with FI.Patients with FI for ≥ 6 months and ≥ 4 moderate or large FI episodes during a 4-week baseline entered a 2-4 week fitting/run-in period to individualise device size (10 or 13 mm) followed by a 4-week treatment period. Outcomes included effectiveness, safety, and quality of life (QoL). The primary outcome was the proportion achieving a ≥ 50% reduction in FI frequency.Of 124 enrolled patients, 98, 71, and 61 progressed through the baseline, fitting/run-in, and treatment phases respectively, with few exclusions due to device intolerance. In the intent-to-treat cohort of 59 participants (93% women), mean (SD) number of days with FI declined from 13.2 (7.0) to 6.3 (6.9), and FI weekly episodes declined from 5.4 (6.9) to 2.1 (5.1) (69% reduction; p < 0.001) with similar results for both device sizes. The primary endpoint was achieved in 76.3% of participants; 54.2% achieved ≥ 75% reduction. The FIQoL overall score increased from a mean (SD) of 1.9 (0.6) to 2.3 (0.6) (p < 0.001), indicating improved QoL. Improvements in FI frequency, FIQoL exceeded minimal clinically important difference thresholds, confirming clear clinical benefit. No treatment-related serious adverse events were reported.The StaySure anal insert device is safe, well tolerated, and effective in reducing FI in patients with moderate to severe symptoms refractory to conservative therapies.ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03898778.© 2026 Mayo Clinic. llm_summary: Faecal incontinence, which is the inability to control bowel movements, affects many people and current treatment options often do not work well enough for those with severe symptoms. Researchers tested a new small device called StaySure that is inserted into the anal canal to help control bowel movements in patients who had experienced at least four episodes of faecal incontinence per week for six months or longer. During the four-week treatment period, patients using the device saw their weekly faecal incontinence episodes drop from an average of 5. 4 down to 2. 1, which represents a 69 percent improvement, and about 76 percent of participants achieved at least a 50 percent reduction in faecal incontinence frequency.

title: Noninvasive Neuromonitoring in Pediatric Traumatic Brain Injury: A Scoping Review of Quantitative Pupillometry and the Evidence Gap in Noninvasive Intracranial Pressure Waveform Analysis.
abstract: Pediatric traumatic brain injury (TBI) is the leading cause of injury-related death and long-term disability in children worldwide. Current monitoring relies predominantly on invasive techniques that carry procedural risks and are not feasible in all settings or across all severity levels. Noninvasive alternatives, including quantitative automated pupillometry and intracranial pressure (ICP) pulse waveform monitoring, have emerged as promising tools, yet their evidence base in pediatric TBI remains uncharacterized. We conducted a scoping review following the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology, reported per Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews, to characterize existing evidence on these two modalities, examining devices, populations, parameters, and key findings. Five databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central, Scopus, CINAHL) were searched through February 2026. Six studies met the inclusion criteria, all addressing quantitative pupillometry. Three evaluated pupillometry in mild TBI in emergency or outpatient settings, one enrolled critically ill children with concurrent invasive ICP monitoring in the pediatric intensive care unit, and two reviewed pupillometry within multimodal neuromonitoring frameworks. All primary studies employed NeurOptics devices. Key findings included time-dependent alterations in pupillary light reflex following concussion and a significant inverse correlation between ICP and pupillometric parameters at thresholds ≥20 mmHg. No primary clinical study evaluated noninvasive ICP pulse waveform morphology devices, specifically P1/P2/P3 analysis characteristic of Brain4care-type technologies in children with TBI. Quantitative pupillometry shows physiologically coherent associations with TBI-related changes, but its utility remains limited by heterogeneous protocols, the absence of age-stratified normative values, and the lack of prospective outcome data. No primary pediatric evidence on noninvasive ICP waveform monitoring was identified, representing the highest-priority evidence gap.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Traumatic brain injury, or damage to the brain from accidents and falls, is the leading cause of injury-related death and long-term disability in children worldwide, making it crucial to find better ways to monitor brain health without invasive procedures. Researchers reviewed six scientific studies to examine two noninvasive monitoring methods, meaning techniques that do not require surgery or insertion of devices into the body: automated pupillometry, which measures how the pupils of the eyes respond to light, and a technique that analyzes the shape of pressure waves in the brain. All six studies focused on pupillometry using devices made by NeurOptics, and researchers found that the pupils showed measurable changes after brain injury and that pupil measurements had a strong inverse relationship with brain pressure when pressure levels were high. However, the review revealed significant gaps in the evidence, particularly that no studies have tested noninvasive brain pressure waveform monitoring devices in children with traumatic brain injury, and that existing pupillometry research lacks standardized protocols and normal reference values for different age groups. title: Neuroprotective Mechanical Ventilation Strategies in Brain-Injured Patients.
abstract: Mechanical ventilation presents a unique challenge in acute brain injury, as lung-protective strategies may adversely affect cerebral physiology. Acute brain injury encompasses a heterogeneous spectrum of disorders with dynamic pathophysiology, precluding uniform ventilatory protocols. The concepts of ventilator-associated brain injury and brain-lung crosstalk underscore the bidirectional impact of mechanical ventilation on pulmonary and neuronal integrity, even in the absence of primary brain pathology but particularly when acute brain injury is present. This article summarizes current evidence on lung-protective ventilation and its cerebral effects, emphasizing high-risk populations. Future research should refine integrated brain-lung protective strategies tailored to each patient's physiologic profile.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Doctors face a difficult problem when treating patients with serious brain injuries because the breathing machines used to protect the lungs can sometimes harm the brain. Brain injuries come in many different types with different causes, so there is no single best way to set up a breathing machine that works for everyone. Researchers in this article looked at how breathing machines affect both the lungs and the brain, explaining that these two organs affect each other in ways we are still learning about. The findings show that doctors need to think carefully about protecting both the lungs and the brain at the same time, especially for patients who are at highest risk of getting worse. Future doctors and researchers should work together to create personalized breathing machine settings that take into account each patient's unique body and brain condition.

title: Optimizing Mechanical Ventilation in Right Heart Failure.
abstract: In patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome, the prevalence of right ventricular dysfunction (RVD) has been documented as high as 60%, though more recent estimates suggest a lower incidence of 20% to 30%, potentially reflecting the broader implementation of lung-protective ventilation strategies. The objective of this article is to review the physiologic principles of mechanical ventilation considering the unique challenges posed by RVD, and to offer a practical bedside approach to optimizing ventilatory support in this patient population. Importantly, mechanical ventilation strategies should aim to protect both the lungs and the heart-in all critically ill patients requiring ventilatory support.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Right heart failure, which is when the right side of the heart cannot pump blood effectively, occurs in a significant number of patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome, a serious lung condition where the lungs cannot deliver enough oxygen to the blood. Previous research suggested that right heart failure happened in up to 60 percent of these patients, but newer estimates show it occurs in only 20 to 30 percent of cases, likely because doctors are now using gentler breathing machine strategies that protect the lungs better. The authors of this article reviewed the basic science behind how mechanical ventilation, or breathing machines, work and explained how to adjust these machines specifically for patients experiencing right heart failure. The key message from this review is that doctors need to think about protecting both the lungs and the heart when deciding how to set up a breathing machine for critically ill patients. This practical guidance helps doctors at the bedside make better decisions about ventilator settings to improve outcomes for patients with this serious complication.

title: Temporary Left Ventricular Assist Devices: Indications and Patient Selection.
abstract: Temporary percutaneous left ventricular assist devices (pLVADs), most prominently transvalvular microaxial flow pumps, have become central tools for contemporary cardiogenic shock care and for hemodynamic protection during selected high-risk percutaneous coronary interventions. Their value, however, is determined far more by patient selection and timing than by device capability alone. This article frames pLVAD use as a high-stakes triage decision anchored in shock phenotype, trajectory, reversibility, and an explicit exit strategy (bridge-to-recovery, bridge-to-decision, bridge-to-transplant, or bridge-to-durable left ventricular assist device).Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Temporary heart pumps, which are small mechanical devices placed inside the heart to help it pump blood, have become important tools for treating patients in severe heart failure or shock. These devices, particularly a type called transvalvular microaxial flow pumps that fit through blood vessels without major surgery, are now commonly used to support patients during emergency heart procedures or when the heart suddenly stops working properly. The success of using these temporary heart pumps depends much more on choosing the right patients and timing the treatment correctly than on the device itself. Doctors must carefully evaluate each patient's condition, including what type of shock they are experiencing, whether their heart might recover on its own, and what the plan is for long-term treatment, such as recovery, transplant, or a permanent heart pump. This approach to patient selection and planning an exit strategy is crucial for improving outcomes and ensuring these powerful tools are used effectively in emergency heart care situations.

title: Permanent Left Ventricular Assist Devices: Long-Term Management and Outcomes.
abstract: This article outlines the historical development, physiologic principles, and contemporary clinical management of durable left ventricular assist devices, with a primary focus on the HeartMate 3 era. An understanding of centrifugal pump physiology, pulsatility index, power, and flow estimation is essential for effective long-term patient management. While major complications such as pump thrombosis and stroke have declined, gastrointestinal bleeding, right ventricular failure, infection, arrhythmias, and outflow graft obstruction remain a significant clinical challenge. Nonetheless, left ventricular assist device therapy as a bridge to transplant, destination therapy, and even recovery are feasible strategies in the context of ongoing donor organ shortages.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Left ventricular assist devices, which are mechanical pumps that help failing hearts pump blood throughout the body, have become increasingly important as a treatment option because there are not enough donor hearts available for transplants. This article reviews how these devices work, focusing on newer models like the HeartMate 3, and explains the key measurements doctors need to understand to manage patients well over the long term. While serious problems like blood clots forming in the pump and strokes have become less common with newer technology, patients still face other significant challenges including bleeding in the digestive system, heart rhythm problems, infections, and blockages in the tubes that carry blood out of the device. Despite these ongoing complications, mechanical heart pump therapy has proven to be a successful approach whether used as a temporary bridge to heart transplant, as a permanent solution for patients who cannot receive a transplant, or even as a way to help some hearts recover enough to work on their own. Future improvements in device design and patient management strategies will be essential to continue improving outcomes as more people rely on these life-saving devices.

llm_summary: Left ventricular assist devices, which are mechanical pumps that help failing hearts pump blood throughout the body, create unique challenges for doctors managing critically ill patients because they produce continuous blood flow rather than the natural pulsing rhythm of a healthy heart. This practical review article was written to help intensive care unit doctors understand how to manage patients using these modern continuous-flow devices by explaining the basic body functions involved and how to troubleshoot common problems. The authors explain that these devices make the heart more sensitive to changes in blood volume and pressure, reduce the natural pulsing of blood in the body, and can affect how well the right side of the heart functions. By understanding how device settings relate to common complications and alarm signals, general intensive care doctors can better care for patients with these mechanical heart pumps and respond more effectively when problems arise. This guide serves as a practical resource to help non-specialist doctors in intensive care units gain the knowledge they need to safely manage patients who depend on these life-saving devices.

title: Noninvasive Ventilation in Chronic Hypercapnic Respiratory Failure.
abstract: Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) is a cornerstone therapy for chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure arising from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS), and neuromuscular disease (NMD). This article reviews the pathophysiology of ventilatory pump failure, key NIV mode features (continuous positive airway pressure, bilevel positive airway pressure-S/ST, volume-assured pressure support, auto-expiratory positive airway pressure), and advanced settings that govern patient-ventilator synchrony. It contrasts respiratory assist devices with home mechanical ventilators and links device choice to disease-specific needs.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Noninvasive ventilation, which means using a mask and machine to help patients breathe without inserting a tube down their throat, is an important treatment for people whose lungs cannot move air in and out properly due to conditions like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, obesity-related breathing problems, or muscle weakness diseases. This article reviews how the breathing muscles fail in these conditions and explains different types of machines and settings that doctors can use to help patients breathe more effectively at home. The authors describe several ventilation modes, which are different ways the machines can deliver air to the lungs, and explain how to adjust advanced settings so that the machine works smoothly with the patient's natural breathing pattern. Understanding which type of machine and settings work best for each disease helps doctors choose the right treatment for their patients and improves their quality of life. This review provides doctors and healthcare providers with practical information to better manage patients with serious long-term breathing problems using noninvasive ventilation instead of more invasive methods.

title: Tailoring disease-modifying therapy approaches across multiple sclerosis sub-populations.
abstract: While advances in anti-inflammatory disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) have transformed multiple sclerosis (MS) care, treatment recommendations are not necessarily applicable or uniform across all populations. This narrative review synthesizes contemporary evidence on DMT selection in people with MS (pwMS) from diverse backgrounds and life stages, accounting for race and ethnicity, reproductive status, age, and sexual and gender identity. We highlight emerging data from clinical trials, post-hoc analyses, and observational studies, offering potential treatment approaches based on the available evidence. llm_summary: Multiple sclerosis is a serious disease affecting the nervous system, and doctors now have many medicines available to slow its progression, but these treatments may not work the same way for everyone depending on their background and life circumstances. Researchers reviewed current scientific evidence to understand how disease-fighting medicines should be chosen differently for people with multiple sclerosis based on factors like race, ethnicity, whether someone wants to have children, age, and gender identity. The review found that recent studies, including detailed analyses of clinical trials and real-world patient data, suggest that treatment recommendations need to be tailored to fit the specific needs and situations of different groups of patients. This research highlights that doctors should consider a patient's individual circumstances when selecting which medicine to prescribe, rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach to treatment. The authors also point out that there are still many unanswered questions about how these medicines work across different populations, meaning more research is needed to improve treatment choices for all patients with multiple sclerosis.

title: Intubation in the Critically Ill: When, How, and How Long?
abstract: Endotracheal intubation is routinely performed in the critically ill setting but carries a high procedural risk and represents a deep cardiorespiratory physiologic impact. Clinical decision to intubate relies heavily on the indication, patient's trajectory, and clinical judgment, rather than rigid cut-offs. Noninvasive ventilation devices are valid methods to delay or avoid intubation in certain clinical scenarios. Before intubation, physiological optimization and personalizing initial ventilatory settings to high-risk patient phenotypes can improve outcomes. Following resolution of the inciting etiology, daily assessment of extubation readiness is essential. llm_summary: Putting a breathing tube down a patient's windpipe, called endotracheal intubation, is a common procedure in hospitals for very sick patients but comes with serious risks and major effects on how the body functions. This review article examines when doctors should decide to place a breathing tube, how they should do it, and how long patients should stay on one. The authors found that the decision to intubate should be based on why the patient needs it, how their condition is changing, and the doctor's judgment rather than following strict numerical rules. Before placing a breathing tube, doctors can improve patient outcomes by preparing the body's systems and adjusting breathing machine settings based on each patient's specific needs and risk factors. Once the original problem causing the illness gets better, doctors need to check every day whether patients are ready to have the breathing tube removed and return to breathing on their own.

title: Patient experiences with pre-abortion healthcare interactions in Ohio, West Virginia, and Kentucky after Dobbs.
abstract: Since the Dobbs decision, abortion seekers have experienced frustration and distress in navigating care within dynamic legal contexts. Pre-abortion interactions with healthcare professionals, such as clinicians and administrative staff working in healthcare settings other than abortion clinics, may play an important role in one's abortion-seeking journey. In this study, we examined how patients perceived the impact of their pre-abortion healthcare interactions when seeking abortion in three states that restricted abortion after Dobbs and how these interactions facilitated or impeded abortion access. Nearly half of interviewees (n = 32/74) interacted with clinicians and/or healthcare administrative staff between pregnancy confirmation and abortion. Of the 52 interactions that participants described, half involved interactions that impeded participants' abortion access, including judgment, dismissal, paternalism, and insufficient or inaccurate information. Participants described feeling distressed by these interactions, occasionally stating that these interactions reduced their trust in their clinician or the medical system. However, just over a third of participants reported abortion-facilitative experiences, receiving encouragement, support, and helpful information about abortion and state laws. Our study adds to the gatekeeping literature and qualitative research on abortion seeker perspectives since Dobbs through analysis of first-hand accounts illuminating the patient experience of navigating care under restrictive and rapidly changing laws and institutional policies. These findings affirm the significance of gatekeepers and facilitators in patient receipt of logistical, informational, and emotional support - be it through healthcare professionals or other sources - in abortion accessibility, particularly for abortion seekers living in abortion restrictive states.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.
