title: Scuba-related injuries presenting to United States emergency departments: paediatric and adult patterns.
abstract: Scuba diving is a popular sport that carries risks unique to the underwater environment. Paediatric emergency department presentations for scuba diving injuries are incompletely characterised, particularly in comparison with adults.We retrospectively analysed scuba-related injuries recorded in the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS) from 2005-2024. We estimated national paediatric emergency department presentations using NEISS weights and compared injury categories and hospitalisation rates between paediatric and adult patients.We identified 68 paediatric cases, corresponding to an estimated 122 paediatric scuba-related emergency department presentations annually. Trauma was the most common injury category (41.2%), followed by otitis (17.6%) and ear, sinus, ocular, or dental barotrauma (16.2%). Hospitalisation was most common among patients with possible decompression sickness or arterial gas embolism (DCS/AGE) (42.9%) and drowning/aspiration (25.0%). Compared with adults, paediatric patients were less often hospitalised (10.3% vs 21.4%, P = 0.038), more likely to present with traumatic injuries (41.2% vs 26.1%, P = 0.010), and less likely to present with possible DCS/AGE (10.3% vs 25.0%, P = 0.006).Among patients presenting to United States emergency departments with scuba-related injuries, paediatric patients most commonly had trauma, otitis, or ear, sinus, ocular, or dental barotrauma. Paediatric divers were also less likely than adults to experience DCS/AGE injuries and were less likely than adults to require hospitalisation. Our data describes emergency department presentation patterns rather than overall injury risk among paediatric scuba divers.Copyright: This article is the copyright of the authors who grant Diving and Hyperbaric Medicine a non-exclusive licence to publish the article in electronic and other forms.

title: Decoding the complexity of tricuspid regurgitation prognostic drivers using explainable artificial intelligence.
abstract: Prognosis in tricuspid regurgitation (TR) is shaped by complex clinical and haemodynamic interactions, complicating risk stratification. We aimed to use explainable artificial intelligence (EAI) to model these relationships and identify key predictors of outcomes.We analysed long-term all-cause mortality in a large prospective registry of patients with native TR across the full severity spectrum. Patients underwent detailed clinical evaluation and quantitative Doppler-echocardiography. Supervised EAI models were applied to identify and rank predictors of mortality under medical therapy, capturing non-linear associations and interactions among baseline characteristics.Among 9761 patients [mean age 73 ± 15 years; 56.9% women; effective regurgitant orifice area (EROA) 40 (30-56) mm2; regurgitant volume 39 (29-53) mL/beat; 42% severe TR], 2676 deaths occurred during 3.8 ± 4.6 years of follow-up. EAI identified and ranked 20 prognostic determinants of survival. Haemodynamic measures, led by elevated pulmonary-artery systolic and right-atrial pressures, were strongest, followed by age and comorbidity. TR-related variables ranked next, led by right ventricular dysfunction and EROA, which outperformed integrative TR grade and TRIScore. Left-ventricular parameters were less influential. Non-linear effects, including those involving ejection fraction, and interactions such as higher EROA-related risk with elevated pulmonary pressures or lower TRIScore (both P < 0.03) were observed. Proportional hazards models confirmed EROA as the strongest TR severity marker (P < 0.0001), with excess mortality beginning at 40 mm2 and increasing further at 60 mm2.EAI ranked mortality predictors in TR, highlighting patient factors, haemodynamics, TR-specific measures, and left-ventricular function. Among TR-specific measures, EROA and TRIScore were most prognostic. title: Spine MRI in Spontaneous Intracranial Hypotension: A Survey of Current State of Practice.
abstract: Spine MRI plays a central role in the diagnostic evaluation of spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH) by helping identify extradural fluid and guide subsequent myelographic technique. Despite its widespread use, the technical details of spine MRI protocols for SIH are often incompletely reported, and the extent of practice variation across specialized centers remains poorly characterized. In addition, ambiguous and inconsistent terminology, including variable use of terms such as "MR myelography" and "heavily T2-weighted MRI," may obscure important differences between non-contrast MRI techniques and examinations performed after intrathecal contrast administration.This State of Practice was developed by neuroradiologists from 9 United States centers with expertise in SIH. Participating centers reviewed and reported their institutional whole-spine MRI protocols for SIH evaluation, including use of 2D and 3D T2-weighted imaging, fat suppression, and echo time.Current spine MRI protocols for SIH show substantial heterogeneity, particularly in fat-suppression technique and echo time, despite universal use of 3D T2-weighted imaging among surveyed centers. Ambiguous terminology further limits comparison across studies and may contribute to confusion regarding whether "MR myelography" refers to non-contrast heavily T2-weighted MRI or intrathecal contrast-enhanced MR myelography. Standardized terminology and more complete reporting of technical parameters are needed to improve interpretation of the literature and guide future protocol refinement.© 2027 by American Journal of Neuroradiology.

title: Ultrasound reference equations for diaphragm thickness and thickening fraction in healthy adults: protocol for an individual participant data meta-analysis.
abstract: Sonographic assessment of diaphragm thickness at end-expiration (DTe) and diaphragm thickening fraction (DTF) is increasingly recognised as a readily available bedside method for evaluating diaphragm structure and function. However, currently available reference values for DTe and DTF vary substantially across populations and between sexes, limiting their clinical interpretability. We hypothesise that an individual participant data meta-analysis (IPD-MA) incorporating readily available anthropometric variables can be used to derive robust population-adjusted ultrasound reference values for DTe and DTF.We will conduct a systematic review and IPD-MA of studies that measured right-sided diaphragm thickness in adult subjects using ultrasound. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection and LILACS/BVS will be searched from inception without language or publication-status restrictions. Anonymised individual participant data will be requested from study authors and harmonised according to a prespecified statistical analysis plan. The primary study aim is to develop prediction equations for DTF and DTe in quietly breathing healthy subjects using linear mixed-effects regression models and derive corresponding 95% reference limits. Model performance and generalisability will be evaluated using internal-external cross-validation. The study is currently at the planning stage-no definitive searches or other formal steps have been performed.Ethical approval is not required for this study as it is based on secondary analysis of anonymised data from previously conducted studies. The findings will be submitted for publication in peer-reviewed journals and disseminated to relevant clinical and research stakeholders.CRD420261321987.© Author(s) (or their employer(s)) 2026. title: Clinical Implications of the Type and Genomic Location of Pathogenic BRCA1 and BRCA2 Variants in Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer.
abstract: Germline pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants (P/LPVs) in BRCA1 and BRCA2 are major determinants of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer susceptibility. Although clinical management has traditionally relied on the presence of a BRCA1/BRCA2 alteration regardless of its specific characteristics, growing evidence suggests that not all BRCA P/LPVs are biologically and clinically equivalent. Variant location within BRCA1 and BRCA2 influences the relative distribution of breast and ovarian cancer risk. Breast cancer cluster regions (BCCRs) are associated with a higher relative risk of breast versus ovarian cancer, whereas ovarian cancer cluster regions (OCCRs), largely encompassing exon 11, are associated with a relative shift toward ovarian cancer risk. Variant type may also be clinically relevant. Protein-truncating P/LPVs have been associated with higher cancer risks than selected missense variants with residual protein function and lower penetrance. Some studies have also reported poorer outcomes for carriers of protein-truncating P/LPVs and more favorable outcomes for those with missense variants. In this narrative review, we summarize current evidence on the clinical implications of BRCA1/BRCA2 P/LPV type and genomic location. While associations between variant location and breast or ovarian cancer risk are supported by large international consortia, prognostic and predictive associations remain largely exploratory. A better understanding of variant-specific genotype-phenotype correlations may ultimately refine risk prediction, preventive strategies, and treatment selection in hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Germline pathogenic variants in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes are known to increase hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk, but clinical management has traditionally treated all variants as equivalent despite emerging evidence suggesting otherwise. This narrative review examined how the specific type and genomic location of BRCA1/BRCA2 variants influence cancer risk patterns and outcomes in affected individuals. The authors found that variants located in breast cancer cluster regions are associated with relatively higher breast cancer risk, while variants in ovarian cancer cluster regions, particularly in exon 11, shift risk toward ovarian cancer; additionally, protein-truncating variants appear linked to higher overall cancer risks and poorer outcomes compared to missense variants with residual protein function. Better characterization of how specific BRCA variants correlate with individual cancer risk patterns could ultimately improve personalized risk prediction, preventive strategies, and treatment selection for carriers of these mutations.

title: Microbiome signatures linked to cancer and treatment adverse events in a real-world cohort.
abstract: The gut microbiome has emerged as a key contributor to cancer biology. Prior studies have focused on individual cancers and often overlook comorbidities, obscuring whether reported associations are specific to a cancer type. Here, we present findings from a real-world mixed-cancer cohort (Mayo Clinic Cancer Microbiome), comprising 1,364 cancer patients and 287 healthy controls. By applying a framework to account for non-specific microbiome associations with cancer, comorbidities, and demographic and clinical variables, we identified 341 cancer-associated species across five cancer classes that represent the most plausible contributors to cancer pathogenesis. Within cancer classes, we found lower levels of fecal bile acids and C. scindens in early-onset breast cancer and elevated lactate and Veillonella parvula in early-onset colorectal cancer. Additionally, Anaerostipes hadrus encoding dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase was protective against 5-fluorouracil-induced diarrhea. These findings demonstrate the strength of our cohort and provide a foundational resource for the discovery of cancer-specific microbiome signatures and predictive biomarkers.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. title: Lessons Learned: Teaching Smarter, Not Harder Through Artificial Intelligence in Instruction.
abstract: Discussions surrounding the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education remain highly prevalent, with most attention focused on how students using AI both within and external to the classroom. title: Accelerated Biological Aging in Cholestatic Liver Disease: Telomere Attrition and Association With Disease Severity.
abstract: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) and primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) are rare, chronic cholestatic liver diseases with heterogeneous progression and limited biomarkers of disease biology. Epigenetic age acceleration has been demonstrated in PSC and PBC, suggesting accelerated biological aging. DNA methylation-derived telomere length (DNAmTL) reflects replicative aging and cellular turnover, but its role in PSC and PBC remains unclear. We aimed to evaluate DNAmTL in PSC and PBC and its association with disease severity.We analysed and compared DNAmTL and age-adjusted DNAmTL among patients with PSC (n = 474) versus PSC controls (n = 484) and patients with PBC (n = 291) versus PBC controls (n = 291). Associations with clinical outcomes were assessed using nonparametric tests and multivariable logistic regression models. Correlations with primary sclerosing cholangitis Risk Estimate Tool (PREsTO) score and epigenetic age acceleration (AgeAccelGrim) were evaluated using linear regression.Patients with PSC demonstrated significantly shorter age-adjusted DNAmTL compared with controls (median -0.036 vs. 0.016, p < 0.001). Patients with PBC also exhibited reduced DNAmTL relative to controls (median 6.814 vs. 6.885, p < 0.001). Within PSC, shorter DNAmTL was associated with cirrhosis (OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.06-0.69, p = 0.013) and advanced disease (OR 0.20, 95% CI 0.06-0.67, p = 0.009). Shorter DNAmTL was also observed in hepatic decompensation and hepatobiliary malignancy, including cholangiocarcinoma. DNAmTL inversely correlated with PReSTO score (p < 0.001). DNAmTL was strongly inversely correlated with AgeAccelGrim in both PSC and PBC (p < 0.001).Cholestatic liver diseases are associated with shortened DNAmTL, which independently correlates with disease severity in PSC. title: The Association Between Hospital Comprehensive Stroke Center Designation Status and Stroke Rate Reporting in the Society of Thoracic Surgeons/American College of Cardiology Transcatheter Valve Therapy Registry After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: Implications for Hospital Performance Assessment.
abstract: The Michigan Structural Heart Consortium showed that transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) stroke rates were associated with hospital Comprehensive Stroke Center (CSC) designation, suggesting that hospital structural factors affect stroke reporting. We sought to determine whether CSC designation is nationally associated with reported stroke rates and the potential impact on hospital performance and Transcatheter Valve Therapy National Data Registry (TVTR) public reporting.Consecutive TVTR cases from January 2016 through June 2023 were included, excluding sites reporting to the TVTR <1 year or performing <20 total TAVR procedures. The primary outcome was in-hospital stroke rate. Secondary outcomes were disabling stroke and 30-day stroke. Major bleeding, death, acute renal failure, and a composite end point were falsification end points to determine whether CSC status was uniquely associated with stroke. Multivariable hierarchical models were created starting with patient covariates and sequentially adding hospital variables to account for determinants of stroke. The impact of CSC status on hospital performance was estimated by correcting CSC hospital stroke rates in the validated TVTR 30-day composite model.A total of 525 919 TAVRs at 800 sites were included, and 10 963 strokes (2.1%) were reported within 30 days: 8284 (1.6%) in-hospital and 2679 (0.5%) after discharge. A total of 4733 (0.9%) were disabling strokes. Multivariate analysis showed that CSC status and participation in TAVR trials were independent predictors of in-hospital stroke rate (P=0.033 and 0.012) and disabling stroke (P=0.033 and 0.007), but not falsification end points (P=NS). Participation in TAVR trials and operator volume were independent predictors of 30-day stroke (P=0.039 and P=0.041). The impact of CSC status on the 30-day composite model showed performance improvement for 8 of 153 CSC hospitals.CSC hospital status and participation in TAVR trials are significant predictors unique for stroke. Correcting for the association of CSC status on stroke rate resulted in an estimated 8 of 153 hospitals improving their TVTR 30-day composite model performance. Further work is needed to account for potential ascertainment bias for stroke in public reporting.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether hospital Comprehensive Stroke Center (CSC) designation—a structural characteristic indicating specialized stroke care capabilities—was associated with differences in reported stroke rates following transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), a minimally invasive heart valve procedure. The study analyzed 525,919 TAVR procedures performed at 800 hospitals between January 2016 and June 2023, finding that 10,963 strokes (2.1%) were reported within 30 days, with 8,284 (1.6%) occurring during hospitalization. When stroke rates were corrected for CSC status in the hospital performance model, only 8 of 153 CSC hospitals showed improved performance rankings, indicating that accounting for this potential reporting bias could modestly affect how hospitals are publicly evaluated. The authors conclude that further investigation.

title: A Cycle of Gendered Vulnerability: Understanding Violence, Poverty, and Systemic Failure Among Refugee Women in Malawi.
abstract: Gender-based violence (GBV) is an urgent global health and social problem. GBV has implications for women's health outcomes and causes disruption to an individual's ecosystem, including their educational attainment, economic stability, and safety. Refugee women are an underserved subpopulation of women who experience extreme vulnerability related to GBV and poor maternal health outcomes. The primary aim of the study was to gain foundational knowledge about the relationship between gender inequality and GBV in the lives of childbearing-aged refugee women in Malawi, including healthcare utilization. Specifically, we sought to (a) explore women's perspectives on the gendered nature of violence, poverty, and vulnerability in the refugee camp context, (b) understand women's experiences and perceptions of health and social services for GBV survivors, and (c) identify structural factors that facilitate or impede women's access to justice and support. Guided by the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), we conducted a qualitative analysis reporting on the qualitative sub-study of a larger mixed-methods project. A total of 50 women were interviewed using focus group discussions from a refugee camp in Malawi on their health, well-being, and experiences with GBV. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings revealed a cycle of gendered poverty, vulnerability, and a gendered system response. The following three subthemes were identified: (a) single motherhood and abandonment as drivers of poverty, (b) marriage as a gendered survival strategy, and (c) the constraining effect of children and caregiving. Poverty is gendered, driven by abandonment, enforced through survivalist marriages, and cemented by caregiving constraints. Systemic responses often replicate the very power imbalances that enable GBV, further perpetuating the cycle. These findings underscore the need for culturally appropriate policies and integrated interventions to address the intersecting social and structural factors contributing to gendered violence, poverty, and vulnerability among refugee women.

llm_summary: Refugee women experience disproportionate vulnerability to gender-based violence, which disrupts their education, economic stability, and safety, yet this population remains understudied in research on violence and health outcomes. Researchers conducted qualitative interviews with 50 childbearing-aged women from a refugee camp in Malawi to understand their experiences with gender-based violence, poverty, and access to health and social services through focus group discussions analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The study identified a cycle in which poverty driven by single motherhood and abandonment pushes women into survivalist marriages, while caregiving responsibilities further constrain their opportunities and independence. Systemic responses to gender-based violence often reinforced existing power imbalances rather than addressing them, thereby perpetuating the conditions that enable violence and vulnerability among refugee women. The findings suggest that addressing gendered violence and poverty among refugee women requires culturally appropriate policies and integrated interventions that target the intersecting social and structural factors underlying these interconnected problems.

title: Updates in the diagnosis of interstitial lung disease: evolving concepts and terminology.
abstract: Interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) comprise a heterogeneous group of disorders that involve the interstitium and may be of identified cause or idiopathic.This review highlights updates in ILD classification and a variety of diagnostic tools. Syndromic classifications including progressive pulmonary fibrosis, systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease-associated ILD, interstitial pneumonia with autoimmune features, and interstitial lung abnormalities are discussed with attention to their clinical utility and limitations. Updates in molecular testing, including genetic testing for telomere-related disorders and telomere length, are discussed along with a brief review of radiomics and its utility in ILD classification and prognostication. We conclude by examining the central role of multidisciplinary discussion in integrating these data into a robust clinical diagnosis.Diagnostic and classification schemes will continue to evolve with diagnostic standards shifting away from lung biopsy to multidisciplinary discussion. Further advances in 'omics' including radiomics and molecular testing will likely aid in classification of disease.

llm_summary: Interstitial lung diseases comprise a diverse group of disorders affecting lung tissue that can have identified or unknown causes, making accurate diagnosis and classification clinically important. This review examines updates in how interstitial lung diseases are classified and diagnosed, including newer syndromic categories such as progressive pulmonary fibrosis, autoimmune-associated interstitial lung disease, and interstitial pneumonia with autoimmune features. The authors discuss advances in molecular testing including genetic testing for telomere-related disorders and telomere length assessment, as well as the emerging role of radiomics in disease classification and predicting patient outcomes. Multidisciplinary discussion integrating clinical, radiological, and molecular data is presented as central to establishing a robust diagnosis, with diagnostic approaches shifting away from reliance on lung biopsy. Future refinements in diagnostic and classification schemes are expected to incorporate advances in molecular testing and radiomics to better characterize and prognosticate interstitial lung disease.

title: Disparities in treatment burden in Peru among people with multiple long-term conditions by geography and healthcare facility: A cross-sectional study.
abstract: People with multiple long-term conditions (MLTC) in low-resource settings face high treatment burdens, influenced by healthcare access and quality disparities. The study aimed to compare the treatment burden among patients with MLTC across geographical locations and healthcare providers in Peru. We conducted a cross-sectional study conducted between June-October 2023 among outpatients aged ≥40 years with type 2 diabetes and ≥1 additional chronic condition, recruited from public and private healthcare facilities in urban Lima and semi-urban Tumbes, Peru. Treatment burden was assessed using the Multimorbidity Treatment Burden Questionnaire (MTBQ). Differences in median MTBQ scores by setting and healthcare provider were analyzed using regression models adjusting for capacity- and workload-related variables. Among 555 participants (55% female, mean age 62.4 ± 10.5 years), median MTBQ score was 27.1 (IQR 14.6-41.7). After adjustment, patients in semi-urban Tumbes had higher treatment burden than those in urban Lima (adjusted median difference 6.1 points; 95% CI 2.9 to 9.3), while patients receiving care in private facilities had lower treatment burden than those in public settings (-6.6 points; 95% CI -9.3 to -3.9). These findings highlight substantial inequalities in treatment burden by place and provider type, with implications for efforts to improve care delivery and reduce disparities for people living with MLTC.Copyright: © 2026 Perez-Leon et al. llm_summary: Researchers examined treatment burden among people with multiple long-term conditions in Peru, comparing differences across geographic locations and healthcare facility types, because patients in low-resource settings often face substantial challenges managing their care. The cross-sectional study enrolled 555 outpatients aged 40 years or older with type 2 diabetes and at least one additional chronic condition from public and private healthcare facilities in urban Lima and semi-urban Tumbes between June and October 2023, measuring treatment burden using the Multimorbidity Treatment Burden Questionnaire. Patients in semi-urban Tumbes reported higher treatment burden than those in urban Lima, with an adjusted median difference of 6.1 points, while patients receiving care in private facilities reported lower treatment burden than those in public settings, with an adjusted median difference of 6.6 points lower. These findings suggest that geographic location and healthcare facility type are associated with meaningful differences in how burdensome patients experience their treatment regimens, pointing to substantial inequalities in care delivery across Peru. The study highlights the need for targeted interventions to reduce treatment burden disparities, particularly in semi-urban areas and public healthcare settings serving people with multiple chronic conditions.
